items.title: Exhibition review: ‘SALT.WIF’ – Stefan Alt’s photography at Galeria ZPAF, Wrocław
items.summary: Karo Kratochwil reviews "SALT.WIF," Stefan Alt's photography exhibition at Galeria ZPAF in Wrocław, part of the 25th Wrocław Industrial Festival.
items.fullText:
Stefan Alt’s photography exhibition “SALT.WIF” opened at Galeria ZPAF in Wrocław on 6 November, presented as part of the 25th anniversary of Wrocław Industrial Festival. It brings together images from different editions of the festival, and there is something fascinating about seeing a concert you remember through another photographer’s eyes. You recognise the musician, perhaps even the gesture, yet the image reveals something you never noticed: a fleeting expression, an unexpected arrangement of light and shadow, a detail that escaped your attention while the music was playing. What once belonged to a familiar experience suddenly looks different.

For many visitors, these photographs offer a view of the festival’s history. For me, they also opened a rather personal conversation with the past.

Stefan Alt, the photographer behind SALT

Stefan Alt, who exhibits and records under the name SALT, is widely recognised as the founder of ant-zen, the German independent label established in 1993. Its catalogue has been influential in industrial, rhythmic noise and experimental electronics, but Stefan’s contribution extends well beyond the records themselves. Photography, graphic design, typography and the physical presentation of releases have long been central to his artistic practice. With ant-zen, the visual identity has never felt like packaging added after the music was finished; it is part of how that music enters the world.

I’ve admired Stefan’s work for years. His album covers, photographic compositions, merchandise and graphic designs have a raw, instantly recognisable beauty, often achieved with remarkably little. A surface, a fragment of an object, the tension between black and white: elements that might appear unremarkable in isolation acquire force through his attention to proportion, texture and detail. There is poetry in his restraint, and sometimes surprising tenderness in images that initially seem severe. I’ve always found that contradiction compelling.

It would be easy to associate such an aesthetic exclusively with the harsher end of industrial culture, but that would miss the curiosity behind it. Stefan does not seem interested in making images that simply look industrial. He is interested in what happens when familiar materials and forms are taken out of their usual context and allowed to suggest something less obvious.

Two rooms, two kinds of attention

The exhibition occupies two rooms, each revealing a different side of his photographic work.

The first is devoted mainly to black-and-white concert images. Against the gallery’s white walls, their deep contrasts immediately command attention, but their graphic strength alone isn’t what makes them interesting. Stefan knows when to let a silhouette dominate a frame, when an expression says more than an entire stage, and how darkness can contribute as much as illumination. Light sometimes isolates a musician from the surroundings; elsewhere it reduces the figure to a form almost abstract in its simplicity.

Anyone who photographs concerts knows how little control we have over the conditions. The lighting changes without warning, movement is unpredictable, and the moment you hope to capture can disappear before you’ve raised the camera. Industrial performances add their own complications: smoke, near-darkness, unconventional staging and projections that compete with the performers for visual attention. Stefan doesn’t try to include everything. He chooses what matters within the frame and lets the rest fall away.

I was struck by how well the photographs worked outside the immediate context of a concert report or an online gallery. At a festival, images are often consumed quickly, surrounded by the noise and excitement of the event. Here I could stand in front of one photograph and consider the space around a figure, the direction of a gesture or the way a single patch of light determined the whole composition.

The pictures retained their connection to the performances, yet did not depend on knowing who was onstage to hold my attention. A live performance is full of sound, movement and successive impressions; a photograph arrests one fraction of it and asks that fraction to stand alone. Sometimes the resulting stillness makes a gesture look more dramatic than it felt at the time. Sometimes it reveals a moment of hesitation or concentration that the speed of the performance concealed. I found myself looking not just at who was depicted, but at what the act of freezing that moment had changed.

The second room offered a different kind of encounter: backstage photographs and portraits of musicians associated with WIF. The intensity of the stage gave way to proximity, familiar faces and quieter moments. Without theatrical lighting or the protective language of performance, the photographer’s attention shifts. The challenge is no longer to capture what an artist does in front of an audience, but to notice something of the person who remains when the performance is over.

A familiar face alone doesn’t make an interesting portrait, and technical perfection doesn’t guarantee that a photograph will say much about its subject either. I am drawn to portraits that resist the easy shorthand of a musician’s public persona and leave room for something less immediately legible.

‘The image begins where recognition ends’

Stefan’s photographs have that quality. They suggest affection and familiarity without becoming sentimental, and an attentiveness to small gestures that might otherwise pass unnoticed. I especially appreciate the absence of any need to turn every musician into an icon. Artists spend so much of their lives constructing a public presence, sometimes quite theatrical on purpose. A photograph can respect that presence while also acknowledging that no person is entirely contained by it. The quieter portraits made me think about how much of a musician’s identity we imagine we know simply because we recognise their face.

His own reflection on portraiture seems especially appropriate here: “The image begins where recognition ends – among those I know, admire, and love.” It speaks to a distinction I think about often in my own work. Photographing someone onstage and photographing that same person away from the performance may involve the same camera, but they require different forms of attention. The first often depends on instinct and anticipation; the second, at its best, on trust and the willingness to look beyond the familiar image.

And then there were the photographs that stopped me for reasons having little to do with composition.

I’ve attended Wrocław Industrial Festival for so many years that some of its performances have become inseparable from particular periods of my life. Walking through the exhibition, I recognised musicians, concerts and moments I had witnessed myself. More than once, I caught myself smiling: I was there.

It was a strangely moving experience. One photograph would bring back a concert; another, a conversation or a face I hadn’t thought about in years. I could remember the music, the atmosphere in the room, sometimes even the people standing nearby. Yet the image in front of me belonged to Stefan’s experience, not mine. He had preserved an instant from a world we had both inhabited, but he had seen it differently. That small distance between his memory and my own was what made the encounter so absorbing.

A photograph might show only the musician, yet bring back things lying completely outside its frame: the anticipation before a performance, the feeling in the room, a brief exchange afterwards. None of those memories had been photographed. Somehow they returned anyway, summoned by an image that was never intended to tell my particular story.

As a photographer, I find this endlessly interesting. Two people can stand only a few metres apart, watching the same performer, and return home with photographs that have almost nothing in common. One notices a movement, another waits for an expression; one embraces the visual chaos, another excludes nearly everything.

Technique matters, of course, especially under difficult concert conditions. But it cannot tell us which moment to care about. That decision comes from experience, curiosity and an instinctive response to the person or scene in front of us. There are also moments when the most honest response is not to press the shutter. Working with a camera can make it tempting to collect evidence of every experience; seeing another photographer’s work reminds me that attention is more complicated than accumulation. What we leave out can be as revealing as what we choose to preserve.

About ‘SALT.WIF’

Stefan’s photographs bear his signature in precisely that sense. Their identity rests less on monochrome contrasts or disciplined compositions than on the choices behind them. The aesthetic is recognisably connected to his graphic work for ant-zen, yet the portraits in particular reveal how flexible that sensibility can be. The imagery associated with industrial music often favours abrasion, distortion and mechanical severity. Here those elements coexist with warmth, vulnerability and an unmistakably human presence.

Seen together, the two rooms tell a richer story than a collection of festival memorabilia could. The concert photographs hold on to the force and theatre of live performance; the portraits remind us of the people behind that intensity. Neither is simply an illustration of industrial culture. They are Stefan’s interpretations of it, built over years of artistic involvement with the music and its community.

That made “SALT.WIF” especially well suited to Wrocław Industrial Festival’s anniversary. Twenty-five editions are not just a succession of lineups. They are also an accumulation of friendships, artistic collaborations, reunions, unexpected encounters and private histories running alongside the public one. A photograph cannot preserve all of that, but it can bring some of it back with startling immediacy.

The vernissage offered a welcome opportunity to experience this history at a different pace. Instead of rushing between concerts or trying to catch the next moment through my own lens, I could spend time with Stefan’s work and with the people gathered around it. Having known his images for so long through records and other music-related publications, I appreciated seeing them occupy a space entirely of their own.

I left the gallery thinking about how much can live inside a photograph without being visible in it. Stefan’s images gave me back concerts, faces and fragments of time I hadn’t realised were still so close. But they also reminded me that remembering is not the same as seeing, and that another artist’s perspective can make even a familiar moment feel newly discovered.

For me, that was the real beauty of the exhibit: not simply looking back at twenty-five years of a festival, but recognising part of my own history through someone else’s eyes.

Photos from the ‘SALT.WIF’ opening

“SALT.WIF” was organised in cooperation with the Consulate General of the Federal Republic of Germany in Wrocław, Galeria ZPAF and Industrial Art. It remains open at Galeria ZPAF, ul. św. Marcina 4, Wrocław, until 29 November 2026, with free admission.

items.title: Tom Shear at 55: celebrating the creative mind behind Assemblage 23
items.summary: American musician and producer Tom Shear, the force behind Assemblage 23, turns 55 on November 12, 2026. A look at his nearly four-decade career.
items.fullText:
American musician, songwriter and producer Tom Shear turns 55 on November 12, 2026. For nearly four decades he has worked under the name Assemblage 23, one of the more recognizable names in electronic body music and futurepop, building a catalogue where club-ready rhythms sit next to intimate, direct songwriting.

Shear was born on November 12, 1971, in State College, Pennsylvania, and developed an early fascination with synthesizers and electronic sound. Largely self-taught, he started experimenting with music well before Assemblage 23 became an established project. A decisive moment came in 1988, when industrial dance music played before a Depeche Mode concert pushed him toward a more rhythmically driven electronic direction.

From ‘Contempt’ to ‘Null’

Assemblage 23 made its official album debut with “Contempt” in 1999, followed by “Failure” in 2001, a record that established Shear’s artistic identity. One of its best-known tracks, “Disappoint,” addressed the loss of his father, and set a pattern that has stayed central to his work: approaching personal, difficult subjects directly rather than hiding them behind the impersonal aesthetics often associated with electronic dance music.

Over the following decades, albums including “Defiance” (2002), “Storm” (2004), “Meta” (2007), “Compass” (2009), “Bruise” (2012), “Endure” (2016) and “Mourn” (2020) expanded the catalogue. Tracks such as “Let the Wind Erase Me,” “Ground,” “Binary” and “Spark” became fixtures of alternative electronic playlists, with each record balancing melodic immediacy against more demanding lyrical material built around vulnerability, loss, alienation and human relationships.

About Tom Shear

Shear’s work beyond Assemblage 23 includes Nerve Filter, a more instrumental and experimental outlet, and Surveillance, which revisits harsher EBM territory. His collaboration with vocalist Mari Kattman as Helix adds trip-hop, dream pop and atmospheric electronics to his range.

In November 2025, Assemblage 23 released “Null,” the project’s tenth studio album, through Metropolis Records, featuring “Believe,” “Tolerate,” “Lunatics” and “Gone.” Speaking to Side-Line in a December 2025 interview, Shear discussed the demanding process of writing lyrics that communicate something meaningful instead of just assembling attractive sounds.

Throughout 2026, Assemblage 23 continued touring North America and Europe, including a run of German and Swedish dates. Shear also contributed guest vocals to Suicide Commando’s single “I Am Your Darkness,” extending his work with other artists across the industrial electronic scene.

As Assemblage 23 approaches four decades of existence, the project’s sound has moved with changes in electronic production and Shear’s own experience while keeping a recognizable identity underneath.

Happy birthday, Tom. Thank you for the music, the honesty and the years of songwriting that have given alternative dancefloors some of their most personal moments. More information is available on the official Assemblage 23 website.

items.title: Chris Connelly at 62: celebrating a life of music, poetry and restless creativity
items.summary: Scottish musician, author and former Fini Tribe member Chris Connelly turned 62 on November 11, 2026. A look back at four decades of restless work.
items.fullText:
Scottish musician, songwriter and author Chris Connelly turned 62 on November 11, 2026. For more than four decades he has followed a musical path that refuses to settle into one genre, from the experimental post-punk of Edinburgh’s Fini Tribe to the industrial machinery of Ministry and Revolting Cocks, and on through an extensive solo career built on literary imagination and collaboration with some of the underground’s most influential musicians.

Connelly was born in Edinburgh on November 11, 1964. He first emerged from Scotland’s experimental underground as a member of Fini Tribe, a collective whose early work combined post-punk, industrial electronics, performance art and a physically demanding approach to live shows. Those formative years carried into his later career: Fini Tribe drew on visual art, experimental theatre and the cultural energy of early-1980s Edinburgh as much as on conventional musical performance.

Speaking to Side-Line in March 2026 alongside fellow Fini Tribe member Andy McGregor, about the retrospective “The Sheer Action of Fini Tribe: 1982-1987”, Connelly described the band’s creative restlessness: “Fini Tribe were never going to settle, we were just too curious.” The remark still describes his career four decades on.

From Edinburgh to Wax Trax! Chicago

His move to Chicago brought him into the orbit of Wax Trax! Records and the network of musicians around Ministry, Revolting Cocks and the emerging American industrial scene. Connelly’s vocals became part of some of the period’s best-known recordings, combining theatrical intensity, aggression and an expressive range that often reached beyond the conventions of industrial rock. His work with Pigface, Murder Inc., The Damage Manual, Acid Horse and, later, Cocksure showed his ability to move between different musical settings without losing his own artistic identity.

That industrial output is only part of the picture. His solo career, beginning with “Whiplash Boychild” in 1991, revealed an artist equally drawn to intimate songwriting, poetry, acoustic instrumentation and the expressive range of his own voice, with influences running from David Bowie and Scott Walker to literary tradition and more experimental composition.

About Chris Connelly

Connelly’s admiration for artists who challenged musical and cultural conventions runs through his more recent work. In 2022, “Eulogy to Christa” explored the life and legacy of Nico through original compositions and reinterpretations of her work. In 2025, “White Phosphorus” returned to the confrontational territory of Throbbing Gristle, one of his formative influences.

He marks this birthday weeks after completing another substantial project. On October 16, 2026, Connelly released “Doo Wop in the Dark: A Portrait of Lou Reed,” a 21-track collection through his own Shipwrecked Industries imprint that pairs reinterpretations of Lou Reed’s music with original compositions tracing Reed’s life and work. The album continues a pattern in Connelly’s output: using artistic biography, interpretation and personal identification to engage with the musicians who influenced him most as a listener.

Alongside his recording career, Connelly is a published author. His memoir, “Concrete, Bulletproof, Invisible & Fried: My Life as a Revolting Cock,” documents the industrial scene’s formative years in Chicago.

At 62, Connelly’s catalogue reads less like a conventional musical career than a continuing record of collaborations, biographical projects and new work, built without treating any of his past output as a finished chapter.

Happy birthday, Chris. Thank you for the music, the poetry and the fascinating conversations that have run through so many different corners of industrial and experimental music.

items.title: Antifer gathers its two EPs on ‘Stella Mantis / Dirty Dents de Scie’ CD
items.summary: Parisian post-punk trio Antifer has compiled its two EPs onto "Stella Mantis / Dirty Dents de Scie," a 16-track CD on Icy Cold Records.
items.fullText:
Parisian post-punk trio Antifer has compiled its two EPs onto “Stella Mantis / Dirty Dents de Scie,” a 16-track CD on Icy Cold Records that adds four further songs to the band’s existing material.

Antifer formed in Paris in 2024 as a trio of Anthony Loridant, Romain Glaser and Carine Rosa. The band wrote, composed and produced the material itself, with mixing and mastering by Fadi Saliba. “Stella Mantis,” the first of the two EPs collected here, came out on Bandcamp on August 21, 2026 with eight tracks: “Stella Mantis,” “Mercredi Noir,” “Grand Voyage,” “Carré,” “L’Ère du Cyclope,” “Le Secret,” “Nos Visions” and “Amor Fati.” The compilation adds “Les Rats,” “Le Sort du Moutard,” “Santa Cruz,” “En Moi Qui,” “Dead Voice / White Noise,” “Existir,” “Anna” and a Lambert version of “Mercredi Noir.” All lyrics are in French, set against post-punk and dark-wave arrangements built around synth lines.

About Antifer

Antifer is a Parisian post-punk and dark-wave trio formed in 2024 by Anthony Loridant, Romain Glaser and Carine Rosa. The band released a run of singles before its first EP, “Stella Mantis,” in 2026, followed shortly after by a second EP. “Stella Mantis / Dirty Dents de Scie” brings both EPs together on CD through Icy Cold Records, alongside four additional tracks not previously collected on one release.

items.title: Varsovie’s ‘Notes pour plus tard’ set for limited vinyl LP on November 27
items.summary: French post-punk band Varsovie's sixth album, "Notes pour plus tard," gets a limited vinyl LP edition on Icy Cold Records on November 27, 2026.
items.fullText:
French post-punk band Varsovie will release its sixth album, “Notes pour plus tard,” on limited black vinyl through Icy Cold Records on November 27, 2026. The album itself came out digitally and on CD on October 16, 2026.

Varsovie recorded “Notes pour plus tard” at Drudenhaus studio in France in August 2025. Grégory Cathérina and Arnault Destal wrote the music, with lyrics by Destal. The album carries French lyrics across eight tracks: “Notes pour plus tard,” “Treize Collines,” “Unica Zürn,” “Partout les chiens,” “Stress,” “1988,” “La Battue” and “Présence.” The band has said “Treize Collines” (“Thirteen Hills,” another name for Paris) alludes to the terrorist attacks of November 13, 2015. Sotiris Lamprou created the album’s artwork.

The vinyl edition is limited to 250 copies on black vinyl with a printed insert.

About Varsovie

Varsovie was formed in Grenoble, France, in 2005 by Arnault Destal (drums, lyrics, music, art direction) and Grégory Cathérina (vocals, guitars, music). The band has released six albums since forming, including “L’Ombre et la Nuit” and 2023’s “Pression à froid,” and has toured across Europe. “Notes pour plus tard” continues the band’s French-language post-punk and dark rock sound, released through Icy Cold Records.

items.title: Gustavo Denouard releases ambient album ‘Escape From The Real World’ on Projekt Records
items.summary: Argentine ambient artist Gustavo Denouard has released his tenth studio album, "Escape From The Real World," on Projekt Records, as a name-your-price download.
items.fullText:
Argentine ambient artist Gustavo Denouard has released his tenth studio album, “Escape From The Real World,” on Projekt Records. The album came out on Bandcamp on September 2, 2026, as a name-your-price digital download, and is his fourth release on the label.

‘Escape From The Real World’ tracklist and credits

The album runs six tracks, organized into three two-part pairs: “An Ocean of Quiet I,” “Floating in the Null I,” “Static Noise of the City I,” “An Ocean of Quiet II,” “Floating in the Null II” and “Static Noise of the City II.” Denouard composed, arranged, performed and produced all the music himself under his Microscope White Noise banner, recording between March and July 2026 with a Korg Wavestate, a Behringer DeepMind 6, a Yamaha DX7 and an Arturia Matrix Minibrute alongside software instruments and effects.

“Escape From The Real World” is available as a name-your-price digital album on Bandcamp.

About Gustavo Denouard

Gustavo Denouard is an Argentine ambient artist who also records under the name Microscope White Noise. “Escape From The Real World” is his tenth studio album and his fourth release through Projekt Records, the Philadelphia-based label known for its catalog of ambient, dark ambient and dream-pop artists. Denouard’s work on the album centers on slow-moving synthesizer pads and hardware sequencing, continuing the label’s long-running focus on atmospheric, drone-adjacent composition.

items.title: MNÆ releases video for ‘Hunt Them All’ ahead of November 13 single
items.summary: German electro trio MNÆ has released the video for "Hunt Them All" on YouTube, ahead of the single's release on November 13, 2026.
items.fullText:
German electro trio MNÆ has released the official video for “Hunt Them All” on YouTube, two days ahead of the track’s release as a single on all platforms on November 13, 2026.

MNÆ builds its sound at the intersection of wave, EBM and modern electro-pop, combining pulsating sequences, distinctive vocals and dark timbres. “Hunt Them All” follows the band’s prior singles “The Lion,” “Hold The Tide” and “Drive.”

“Hunt Them All” will be available on all major streaming and download platforms from November 13, 2026, alongside Bandcamp.

About MNÆ

MNÆ formed in 2026 as a trio of Arc Morten, Jan Wilking and Axel Tasler. Morten also records as Cyto and Morphose, Wilking as Steril and EvvilKing, and Tasler as Steril and Audiocall. The band released its debut single “The Lion” in 2026, followed by “Hold The Tide,” which also appeared in a club edit by EvvilKing, and “Drive.” “Hunt Them All” is the band’s fourth single, previewed with a teaser clip before the full video’s release on November 11, 2026, two days ahead of the single itself.

items.title: ‘Sinapsa Insekta’ brings insect bioacoustics and EEG data to Nova Gorica
items.summary: Martina Testen and Simon Šerc present "Sinapsa Insekta," an interactive installation combining insect field recordings and EEG data, at EPICenter Nova Gorica.
items.fullText:
Slovenian artists Martina Testen and Simon Šerc are presenting “Sinapsa Insekta,” an interactive audiovisual installation, at EPICenter in Nova Gorica from 6 to 13 November 2026. The piece premiered to the public on 6 November at 7:00 PM and runs through 13 November at 5:00 PM.

How ‘Sinapsa Insekta’ works

“Sinapsa Insekta” is built on field recordings of insect sounds captured on the Banjšice Plateau in Slovenia. Visitors wear EEG electrodes that let their brain activity adjust the sound filters, rhythms and frequencies drawn from those recordings, while motion sensors track their movement through the space. Both data streams feed a custom computer program that alters the soundscape in real time and generates synapse-like visual structures on screen.

The name “Sinapsa Insekta” dates back three years, to a short animated film Testen and Šerc entered in the first edition of an artificial intelligence festival in South Korea, where it won an award. The pair expanded that concept into the current interactive installation, combining intermedia art, biometric data, sound and generative visuals. “Sinapsa Insekta” received support from the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Slovenia and the Municipality of Nova Gorica.

About Martina Testen and Simon Šerc

Testen and Šerc work together as Biodukt, a field recording and sound art project, across sound art, video, field recordings and interactive technology, with a recurring focus on perception, time and the relationship between humans and the natural environment. Their field recording releases have been covered by outlets including The Guardian, BBC and The Wire, and their audiovisual work has received international awards.

“Sinapsa Insekta” extends that practice, carrying their Banjšice Plateau field recordings into an interactive format for the first time. The installation remains on view at EPICenter in Nova Gorica, Slovenia, through 13 November 2026.

items.title: Benjamin Russell releases ‘Elemental’ album on TCBE Records
items.summary: Montreal singer-songwriter Benjamin Russell has released "Elemental," a 10-track album produced with longtime collaborator Elyce, out now on TCBE Records.
items.fullText:
Montreal singer-songwriter Benjamin Russell has released “Elemental,” a ten-track album on TCBE Records. The album arrived on Bandcamp on November 4, 2026, and was produced by Russell with Elyce, his longtime collaborator and co-writer.

“Elemental” follows 2025’s “Waves” and continues the acoustic-and-electric, synth-and-drum-machine approach of that album. Russell wrote and recorded it during his own diagnosis and treatment for pancreatic cancer, according to his press materials.

The tracklist runs: “Flying (Volo Volare Mix),” “Elemental,” “Gyro,” “Eternity,” “Not Alone,” “Empathy,” “Ordinary Man,” “Time and Tide,” “Pillow Talk” and “Bittersweet.” Elyce and Russell share the production and lyric-writing credit; Russell plays electric and acoustic guitars, synths and drum machines, and handles all lead and background vocals.

Sandy Miss Parker of Rave and Roll Blog reviewed the album ahead of release, describing its vocal performances and arrangement: “I really love this album – Elemental. It’s his best yet. The vocals are strong and the instrumentation is layered beautifully. Plus, I’m a synth nerd and it tickles that part of me too!”

“Elemental” is available as a digital album on Bandcamp.

About Benjamin Russell

Benjamin Russell is a singer-songwriter, painter, graphic artist, videographer and writer based in Montreal, Quebec. His recorded output stretches back to 1980s releases including “Madman” and “Notes From Underground,” followed by “Rockhill” in 2010 and “Sundog” in 2013.

After a hiatus during which he focused on painting, Russell returned to music at the end of 2019 with “Shikasta Suite,” a rock opera written with Elyce. Albums and EPs through TCBE Records followed at a steady pace: “Balance” (2020), “Something In F Minor” and “Brighter Light” with Rob Stuart (2023), “Frontier” (2023), “GHOST PARTICLES” with Greg Fraser (2024), “Pleasure Center” (2024) and “Waves” (2025).

Russell describes “Elemental” as a record drawing on pop, punk, opera, jazz, folk, ambient, rock, electronic and classical influences. It is available now on Bandcamp.

items.title: Sever Synth Fest 2027: Laibach and Die Krupps headline fifth anniversary in Liberec
items.summary: Sever Synth Fest 2027 brings Laibach, Die Krupps and Assemblage 23 to Liberec, Czech Republic, for its fifth anniversary on 5-6 November.
items.fullText:
Sever Synth Fest will celebrate its fifth edition on 5-6 November 2027 in Liberec, Czech Republic. Laibach, Die Krupps and Assemblage 23 head the lineup, alongside Diorama and In Strict Confidence.

The main programme takes place on Saturday, 6 November, at Dům kultury Liberec. A separate warm-up evening at Club Warehouse on Friday, 5 November, introduces four further international acts.

Lineup for Sever Synth Fest 2027

Laibach, the Slovenian collective associated with the Neue Slowenische Kunst movement, has worked at the intersection of music, conceptual art, political commentary and theatrical provocation since forming in 1980. German industrial group Die Krupps emerged from Düsseldorf’s post-punk scene in the early 1980s, building a vocabulary around mechanical percussion, electronic sequencing and industrial rock guitar under Jürgen Engler.

American project Assemblage 23, founded by Tom Shear, combines programming and club rhythms with direct songwriting. Its 2025 album “Null” continued a catalogue centered on psychological struggle and human relationships. Germany’s In Strict Confidence, led by Dennis Ostermann, brings dark electro and theatrical arrangements. The project’s newly announced album “The Final Kiss” follows releases including “Cryogenix,” “Face the Fear” and “Love Kills!”

Diorama, led by Torben Wendt, moves between darkwave, alternative electronics and experimental composition. Its 2026 album “A Substitute for Light” addresses perception and technological alienation. German synthpop act Beborn Beton, whose album “Darkness Falls Again” paired melodic songwriting with serious subject matter, also appears on the bill, alongside CHROM, the EBM project led by Christian Marquis.

Dutch act Angels & Agony, founded by Reinier Kahle in 1995, contributes futurepop and darkwave with spiritual lyrical themes. Czech act Lakeside X, fronted by Janne Marvannen, collaborated with Daniel Myer on the album “Love Disappears” and released “Absinthe Dream” in 2026.

The Friday warm-up at Club Warehouse opens with Canadian synthpop project Trans-X, founded by Pascal Languirand and known for “Living on Video.” Spain’s Culture Kultür brings its 2026 album “Atomic,” addressing human relationships and technological alienation more than three decades after the project’s formation. British act j:dead, created by Jay Taylor, and Belarusian industrial duo Ambassador21 complete the warm-up lineup.

Dates and venues for Sever Synth Fest 2027

Warm-up: Friday, 5 November 2027, Club Warehouse, Liberec, Czech Republic. Trans-X (CA), Culture Kultür (ES), j:dead (UK), Ambassador21 (BY).

Main festival: Saturday, 6 November 2027, Dům kultury Liberec, Czech Republic. Laibach (SI), Die Krupps (DE), Assemblage 23 (US), CHROM (DE), Diorama (DE), In Strict Confidence (DE), Angels & Agony (NL), Beborn Beton (DE), Lakeside X (CZ).

More information is available on the festival website.

About Sever Synth Fest

Sever Synth Fest is held annually in Liberec, Czech Republic. The 2027 edition is the festival’s fifth, expanding to two evenings across two venues, Dům kultury Liberec and Club Warehouse, with thirteen international acts spanning industrial, EBM, synthpop and futurepop.

items.title: Sznur sets ‘Bloki z betonu i ciał’ CD on Raubbau
items.summary: Polish power electronics act Sznur releases the CD "Bloki z betonu i ciał" via Raubbau on November 17, 2026, with layout by Stefan Alt.
items.fullText:
Polish power electronics and death industrial act Sznur will release the CD “Bloki z betonu i ciał” through Raubbau on November 17, 2026. The eight-track release is issued in a matte six-panel digipak, with layout by Stefan Alt.

Tracklist for ‘Bloki z betonu i ciał’

The album runs eight tracks: “Bez Tytułu,” “Czerń,” “Obca Twarz,” “Gorycz,” “Algorytm Bólu,” “Gasnąć,” “Stalowy Bóg” and “Smak Potępienia.” It combines power electronics with dark ambient textures and death industrial elements. Sznur recorded the album in February 2025; Kacper Pawluk handled recording, engineering, mixing and mastering.

“Bloki z betonu i ciał” is available to pre-order as a digipak CD and digital album on Bandcamp, through Berlin-based label Raubbau.

About Sznur

Sznur is a power electronics and death industrial act from Poland, performing as Tomek, Vlad and Kuba. “Bloki z betonu i ciał,” released through Raubbau, continues the project’s work within that scene, built around dense, abrasive sonic arrangements.

items.title: Violet Nox releases ‘Spectre’ remix by Black Snow On Christmas
items.summary: Violet Nox releases a remix of "Spectre" by Black Snow On Christmas, out 5 November 2026 on Bandcamp, with a new video directed by Allison Tanenhaus.
items.fullText:
Boston dark wave trio Violet Nox has released a remix of “Spectre,” reworked by German musician Chris Wirrwitz under his project name Black Snow On Christmas. The digital single came out on Bandcamp on 5 November 2026, with a new video following days later.

“Spectre” is the opening track of Violet Nox’s eighth album, “Silvae,” released in late 2025 through Somewherecold Records. The remix keeps the original’s core elements, written by Dez DeCarlo and Andrew Abrahamson with vocals and lyrics by Noell Dorsey, while Wirrwitz builds a new production around it. DeCarlo and Abrahamson contributed additional production to the remix, which Abrahamson also mastered.

The accompanying video was directed by Allison Tanenhaus, who also designed the cover art for both the remix and the “Silvae” album.

“Spectre (Remix by Black Snow On Christmas)” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp.

About Violet Nox

Violet Nox is a trio from Boston, Massachusetts, built around synthesists Dez DeCarlo and Andrew Abrahamson and vocalist Noell Dorsey. The group works across dark wave, cold wave, ambient and drone, built from synthesis, samples and effects pedals. “Silvae,” released in late 2025 through Somewherecold Records, is the band’s eighth album together, recorded, mixed and mastered by DeCarlo and Abrahamson in Boston. Its opening track, “Spectre,” is the source for this new remix by Black Snow On Christmas, released on Bandcamp on 5 November 2026.

items.title: Majestic Phoenix and CZARINA release ‘Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix)’
items.summary: CZARINA and Majestic Phoenix release the darkwave single 'Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix)', out 10 November 2026 on Bandcamp, with a new video.
items.fullText:
American electropop duo Majestic Phoenix and darkwave artist CZARINA have released “Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix),” a collaborative reworking of Majestic Phoenix’s original track. The digital release went out on Bandcamp on 10 November 2026, alongside a new music video.

CZARINA contributes new vocals, lyrics and instrumentation to Majestic Phoenix’s original composition. The two-track release pairs the vocal version with an instrumental mix, mixed and mastered in analog by Von Hertzog at The Social Club. “Angels + Demons” first appeared as a Majestic Phoenix original in August 2026, following an earlier version featuring Emy Smith in July.

The accompanying video was produced and directed by The Kitsunés, the creative partnership of CZARINA and her husband, visual artist Carlos Kitsuné. Filmed in Malpica de Bergantiños, on Galicia’s Costa da Morte, it follows a pilgrim on the Camino de Santiago who encounters the Devil, drawing visual reference from Ingmar Bergman’s 1957 film “The Seventh Seal” and Friedrich Moritz August Retzsch’s 1831 painting “Die Schachspieler” (“The Devil’s Checkmate” in English).

“Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix)” is available as a digital release on Bandcamp.

About CZARINA

CZARINA, the recording name of Vero Faye Kitsuné, is an American singer, producer, composer, multi-instrumentalist and filmmaker. Born in the Philippines and raised in New York, she now lives on Spain’s Costa da Morte, in Galicia. She began recording as CZARINA in 2018, working across dark electro and darkwave.

Side-Line first covered CZARINA in March 2021 with the dark electro single “Atomic: Ad Initivm.” A year later, in March 2022, she released the album “Arcana,” the source material for the remix now released with Majestic Phoenix, and sat down with Side-Line that June for an interview about her creative process. In 2025, she announced the 7CD post-punk box set “Resurgence,” compiling earlier material. CZARINA directs her own videos under the name The Kitsunés, a partnership with her husband, artist Carlos Kitsuné, which also made the video for “Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix).”

About Majestic Phoenix

Majestic Phoenix is an American electronic duo formed by Aaron McLean and Kent “Von” Hertzog, based in Maryland. McLean writes, performs and produces the group’s songs; Hertzog co-produces, mixes and masters them at his studio, The Social Club. The two met at the Art Institute of Philadelphia in 1999. Majestic Phoenix released its debut EP, “Manifest,” in October 2025, followed by a run of singles through 2026 including “Crystal,” “I Rise (Chaos, Reimagined)” and two versions of “Angels + Demons,” the song CZARINA reworks on this release.

items.title: Esplendor Geométrico reissues ‘Comisario de la Luz / Blanco de Fuerza’ as an expanded 2LP
items.summary: Esplendor Geométrico's 1985 album "Comisario de la Luz / Blanco de Fuerza" returns on Geometrik as a limited, expanded 2LP with bonus rarities.
items.fullText:
Esplendor Geométrico’s 1985 album Comisario de la Luz / Blanco de Fuerza returns on Geometrik Records as a limited, expanded 2LP. The Madrid industrial duo’s second album has been unavailable on vinyl for more than 15 years; this edition adds a bonus LP of rarities from the band’s 1980s tape and compilation output.

“Comisario de la Luz / Blanco de Fuerza” followed Esplendor Geométrico’s 1982 debut “Héroe del Trabajo / El Acero del Partido” and arrived in 1985, during the band’s noisiest, darkest period. The album combines subsonic frequencies (“Comisario de la Luz II”), minimal noise rhythms (“Blanco de Fuerza II”) and distorted melodic lines (“Blanco de Fuerza III”).

The expanded edition’s bonus LP (Side C) collects four tracks that originally appeared on the compilation “Bruitiste” (RRRecords, 1988), a double LP that some listeners consider among the strongest material Esplendor Geométrico recorded in its first decade. Side D adds further 1980s recordings that had previously surfaced only on CD compilations.

The reissue was remastered in 2026 by Luca Spagnoletti from the original 1983-1988 Madrid recording sessions. Design is by Alonso Urbanos, with images by Andrés Noarbe. The vinyl is limited to 500 copies on black vinyl.

‘Comisario de la Luz / Blanco de Fuerza’ tracklist

A1 Comisario de la Luz I A2 Comisario de la Luz II A3 Comisario de la Luz III A4 Comisario de la Luz IV B1 Blanco de Fuerza I B2 Blanco de Fuerza II B3 Blanco de Fuerza III B4 Blanco de Fuerza IV C1 Nitr. I C2 Nitr. II C3 Nitr. III C4 Nitr. IV D1 Avance Rápido D2 Raskin D3 Comisario de la Luz V D4 Primera Tundra

Esplendor Geométrico was formed in Madrid by Arturo Lanz and Gabriel Riaza, who led the band through this period between 1982 and 1991. Side-Line has previously covered the band’s archival reissue campaign on Geometrik, including the 2021 vinyl editions of “Live in Utrecht” and the 40th-anniversary “EG-1”, and 2019’s double-vinyl treatment of “Selected Tracks 2 (1995-1998)”.

About Esplendor Geométrico

Esplendor Geométrico formed in Madrid in 1980, building a harsh, mechanical strain of industrial music out of cheap synthesizers, tape loops and distorted rhythm. The band released its debut single, “Necrosis en la Poya”, in 1981, followed the same year by the cassette “EG-1”. Arturo Lanz and Gabriel Riaza led the band through the 1980s, releasing the debut album “Héroe del Trabajo / El Acero del Partido” in 1982 and “Comisario de la Luz / Blanco de Fuerza” in 1985.

The band founded its own label, Geometrik Records, to document its catalogue and reissue archival material. Since the 2010s, Geometrik has issued a steady run of vinyl reissues and rarities collections, including “Fungus Cerebri (Selected Tracks From Cassettes 1981-1989)” in 2016, the 35th-anniversary boxset “Selected Tracks 1: 1992-1998” in 2015, and expanded vinyl editions of “Live in Utrecht” and “EG-1” in 2021. The expanded “Comisario de la Luz / Blanco de Fuerza” is the label’s latest entry in that reissue campaign, bringing one of the band’s mid-1980s albums back into print with previously tape-only and compilation-only material attached.

items.title: Rome’s ‘Die Æsthetik der Herrschaftsfreiheit’ turns 15 on 11 November
items.summary: Rome released the trilogy "Die Æsthetik der Herrschaftsfreiheit" through Trisol on 11 November 2011. The three-volume album turns 15 this year.
items.fullText:
Luxembourgish neofolk act Rome released the three-volume album “Die Æsthetik der Herrschaftsfreiheit” through Trisol on 11 November 2011. “Die Æsthetik der Herrschaftsfreiheit” turns 15 this year.

Jérôme Reuter, Rome’s sole constant member, built the record as a 36-track trilogy split into three twelve-track volumes: “Aufbruch” (“A Cross of Wheat”), “Aufruhr” (“A Cross of Fire”) and “Aufgabe” (“A Cross of Flowers”). The lyrics draw on the writings of Bertolt Brecht, Pablo Neruda, Hans Magnus Enzensberger and Gustav Landauer, worked through Rome’s mix of neofolk, martial industrial, dark ambient and chanson. It was the first Rome album recorded with analogue technique and minimal post-production.

Trisol issued the trilogy as a limited box set in November 2011, then released the three volumes separately on CD in 2012. Side-Line covered a three-LP vinyl reissue of the set in 2017, and COP International currently offers a signed, limited clear-vinyl 3LP edition capped at 500 copies worldwide. All three volumes of “Die Æsthetik der Herrschaftsfreiheit” stream on Spotify.

About Rome

Rome is a neofolk project from Luxembourg, formed in November 2005 by Jérôme Reuter as the main outlet for his songs. Reuter recorded Rome’s first release, the EP “Berlin,” in December 2005 at sound engineer Patrick Damiani’s studio in Germany. Rome signed to the Swedish label Cold Meat Industry in early 2006 and released the debut album “Nera” that year, followed by “Confessions d’un voleur d’âmes” (2007) and “Masse Mensch Material” (2008). Damiani became a full-time member of Rome in 2008, and violinist Nikos Mavridis joined in 2009, the same year Rome signed to Trisol Music Group and released “Flowers from Exile.” “Nos Chants perdus” followed in 2010, before “Die Æsthetik der Herrschaftsfreiheit” arrived as a trilogy box set in November 2011.

Rome continued with “Hell Money” (2012), “A Passage to Rhodesia” (2014), “Coriolan” and “The Hyperion Machine” (both 2016), and further albums including “Hall of Thatch” (2018), “The Lone Furrow” (2020), “Parlez-Vous Hate?” (2021) and “Hegemonikon” (2022). “Gates of Europe” followed in 2023, and Rome released “Civitas Solis,” “The Tower” and “The Hierophant” in 2025. Fifteen years after its release, “Die Æsthetik der Herrschaftsfreiheit” remains Rome’s largest release to date, at 36 tracks across three volumes.

items.title: Phosgore – Priority Targets (Digital/CD Album – ProNoize / Dark Dimensions)
items.summary: I generally avoid paying much attention to compilations, but occasionally I’m happy to make an...
items.fullText:
I generally avoid paying much attention to compilations, but occasionally I’m happy to make an exception—as is the case with “Priority Targets” by the German duo Phosgore. Aside from the single “Slaves To The Bassline,” released last year, Florian and Sonja Dietz hadn’t released any new material since “Pestbringer”, their third album, back in 2015. This compilation brings together tracks from their three albums and two singles.

It’s a great opportunity for Electro fans who aren’t yet familiar with the band to discover their sound: a harsh, relentless production style that blends Dark-Electro and Industrial-Techno into a hard-hitting, highly danceable experience. There are no conventional vocals, apart from the occasional spoken-word sample. The sound is often raw, with layers of icy sequences taking the place of traditional melodies. Phosgore’s back catalogue contains plenty of fantastic tracks, and bringing them together here results in a heavy, pounding, dance-oriented collection that is perfectly suited to Industrial dance floors. While the formula can occasionally feel a little simplistic or even somewhat dated, Phosgore remains an important reference point within this particular corner of the Electro scene—a niche in which, in my view, Noisuf-X has always been the ultimate benchmark.

It would be difficult to claim that Phosgore is truly ‘back’, but hopefully, this release will pave the way for some entirely new material. I certainly miss this band! (Rating:8½).

Listen to “VX”:

About Phosgore

Phosgore is the German project of Florian Dietz and Sonja Dietz, working in an industrial-rave and dark-electro-techno style geared toward the dancefloor. The duo built a catalogue through the albums “Domination”, “Warhead” and “Pestbringer” (2015), alongside EPs including “Slaves to the Bassline” and “Noise Cannon”. The band records for Pro Noize, the Dark Dimensions sub-label that also hosts Noisuf-X, and “Priority Targets” draws that output together into a single limited release.

items.title: “Do You Believe?” — Los Angeles Ethereal Goth Artist Rose Haze Summons Celestial Visitors in Video for “They Are Here”
items.summary: Take us to nirvana, Celestial cosmonaut Teach us Galactic truth Looking into a night sky, it is easy to see how the stars became a place to put our questions.… The post “Do You Believe?” — Los Angeles Ethereal Goth Artist Rose Haze Summons Celestial Visitors i
items.fullText:
Take us to nirvana, Celestial cosmonaut
Teach us Galactic truth 

Looking into a night sky, it is easy to see how the stars became a place to put our questions. We draw figures between distant points of light, imagine gods moving among them, and wonder whether someone out there might know more about our lives than we do. The celestial visitors of alien mythology inherit that mixture of curiosity and longing: they may bring knowledge, promise deliverance, or announce that our time has run out. Much depends on which message we are willing to believe.

That primeval appetite for revelation runs through They Are Here, the new single from Rose Haze, the project of Los Angeles songwriter, multi-instrumentalist, and producer Kate Ramsey. Accompanied by an animated video from Japhy Riddle, the song sends ethereal goth, shoegaze, and psychedelia into a sky crowded with competing promises of salvation.

A rushing surge gives way to a deep post-punk bassline and drums that shudder with slow tension. Heavy guitar presses into the spaces around them, while a buzzing synth melody appears and recedes like small lights crossing the dark. Ramsey’s cool, airborne vocals suggest The Shroud and the more spectral reaches of the Projekt Records catalogue, carrying a melody whose beauty makes the unfolding catastrophe all the more unsettling.

As the arrangement expands, the guitars approach the luxuriant heights of Cocteau Twins and the gothic grandeur of Faith and the Muse. They shiver and crash, at moments acquiring the reedy, massed cry of bagpipes. The bass keeps a firm foothold beneath all that upward movement, giving the song a physical weight equal to its celestial ambitions.

Ramsey’s lyrics gather burning forests, the falling Wormwood star, a drying Euphrates, and creatures assembled from horses, locusts, and scorpions. Biblical catastrophe becomes entangled with bodily possession and appeals to a “Celestial cosmonaut.” The mingling of divine visitation and alien arrival evokes the ancient-astronaut speculation of Erich von Däniken’s Chariots of the Gods, with sacred imagery reconsidered as possible extraterrestrial contact. Yet the early warning, “False prophets seduce the weak,” hangs over every promised revelation. Each return of “Do you believe?” tests the distance between wanting an answer and trusting whoever offers one.

Riddle gives this uncertainty a wonderfully strange visual form. Pale, chalk-like contours turn bodies, beasts, spacecraft, and machinery into moving constellations. A hooded preacher addresses a congregation of sheep; screens repeat his image, and disembodied lips multiply across the darkness. Horsemen rise through a violet sky while forests burn below. The imagery suggests a universe in which belief travels through broadcasts, symbols, and spectacles, with every apparent revelation raising another question about who controls the picture.

Those expressive outlines recall Emily Hubley’s animation for The Origin of Love in Hedwig and the Angry Inch, where drawn figures give an ancient myth about human longing an immediate emotional life. Riddle’s figures likewise seem to belong to a story being written across the heavens. Their spare forms make the immense scale approachable, allowing the viewer to follow a gesture or a face through the surrounding cosmic machinery.

Eventually, the darkness opens onto a pastel heaven of clouds, floating crystals, and sheep. Its sweetness proves unstable: the scene resolves into a wireframe image on an old computer monitor, which goes blank. “The simulation has come to an end,” Ramsey sings. After all those appeals to higher powers, the film leaves us looking at the apparatus that contained their universe.

The closing dedication brings the film back to a deeply personal loss. They Are Here features the late guitarist Ruben Gonzales, Ramsey’s close collaborator, who died in 2024. His guitar parts date to the earliest sessions for the forthcoming album, which Ramsey finished alone after his death. The force of his playing gives this vast journey an intimate center: within its visions of endings and escape, the recording preserves the work they began together.

Watch the video for They Are Here below:

They Are Here is the lead single from Rose Haze’s forthcoming album, A Whole Lot of Nothing for No One, out January 31, 2027. Her first full-length album in five years is available to pre-order here. In the meantime, listen to They Are Here below:

Born in Ohio, Ramsey plays piano, synth, guitar, harp, bass, and flute. She recorded and performed her first two albums with Lisa Bella Donna, later traveling through Europe and Kaua’i before moving to California in 2019, where she met Gonzales. Her live performances make room for improvisation and changing instrumental combinations, allowing the songs to shift shape from one set to the next.

Riddle is an animator and musician whose interests in science, mathematics, and computer engineering inform his visual work.

items.title: The Devil’s Checkmate — Majestic Phoenix and CZARINA Play an Infernal Game in Video for “Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix)”
items.summary: Take my hand Angels and demons have tried We create our own design The Devil has always been an enthusiastic gambler, particularly when the stakes involve somebody else’s eternal future.… The post The Devil’s Checkmate — Majestic Phoenix and CZARINA Play an In
items.fullText:
Take my hand

Angels and demons have tried

We create our own design

The Devil has always been an enthusiastic gambler, particularly when the stakes involve somebody else’s eternal future. Across centuries of folklore, he has appeared at crossroads, in taverns, and beside the beds of ambitious men, offering arrangements whose disadvantages become apparent around the time the contract comes due. Chess, with its elaborate rules and opportunities for deception, seems particularly suited to his temperament. Every sacrifice has a purpose, every advance invites retaliation, and the unfortunate soul across the board must calculate how much of himself he can afford to lose.

In Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix), Galicia-based American darkwave artist C Z A R I N A revisits the work of American cinematic electropop duo Majestic Phoenix, contributing her own vocals, lyrics, and instrumentation to a composition concerned with fate, spiritual transformation, and the difficult business of deciding who gets to govern one’s existence.

C Z A R I N A’s interpretation supplies the confrontation with an appropriately extravagant musical vocabulary. Her commanding voice rises through theatrical electronic arrangements, drawing upon the dramatic sensibilities of Kate Bush, the ethereal grandeur of Lisa Gerrard, and the widescreen emotional sweep of Florence + The Machine. The music suggests an occult fairy tale unfolding at the edge of the known world, where every melodic ascent carries the possibility of revelation.

Produced and directed by The Kitsunés, the accompanying video pays homage to Ingmar Bergman’s The Seventh Seal (1957), while drawing inspiration from Friedrich Moritz August Retzsch’s 1831 painting The Devil’s Checkmate, originally titled Die Schachspieler. Retzsch’s painting depicts a young man facing Satan across a chessboard, his immortal soul hanging in the balance as his adversary surveys the pieces with the confidence of someone who already knows the outcome. Bergman would later explore a similar predicament through a medieval knight who challenges Death to a game of chess, hoping to bargain for a little more time. Both works contemplate the uneasy relationship between free will and fate, raising a question that has troubled theologians, philosophers, and gamblers for centuries: how much freedom does a person possess when the rules have been established by somebody else?

The filmmakers transport this confrontation to Malpica de Bergantiños, along Galicia’s formidable Costa da Morte, where the Atlantic crashes against ancient coastal formations. A pilgrim travelling the Camino de Santiago encounters the Devil, and his spiritual expedition takes an unexpected detour into supernatural competition. Against the vastness of the coastline, their chessboard becomes a miniature arena for mankind’s oldest anxieties about temptation, judgment, and the possibility of redemption.

The video’s central wager also illuminates the remix’s larger preoccupation with inherited beliefs. To abandon an old conviction can resemble a small death; to replace it requires imagination, courage, and occasionally a willingness to disappoint the authorities, earthly or otherwise, who benefited from one’s obedience. At the Devil’s chessboard, destiny appears to have been calculated in advance. C Z A R I N A leaves us contemplating the delicious possibility that the pilgrim might yet overturn the board.

Watch the video for “Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix)” below:

Listen to Angels + Demons (Arcana Remix) below and order it here.

C Z A R I N A is the musical project of Vero Faye Kitsuné, a Philippine-born, New York-raised American singer, producer, composer, multi-instrumentalist, and filmmaker now based on Galicia’s Costa da Morte. Her background spans music, visual art, and a career as a fashion designer and creative director. Since her recording debut in 2018, she has developed an elaborate musical language encompassing gothic post-metal, orchestral darkwave, and ethereal dark synthpop, combining the weight of metal with orchestral arrangements and dark electronic textures. Mysticism, mythology, and alchemy inform her recordings and films, while cosmic and celestial imagery accompanies her explorations of destruction, transformation, rebirth, and transcendence. Albums including Arcana (2022) and Empire explore these interests on an increasingly ambitious scale. Alongside her husband, artist Carlos Kitsuné, also known as DeadlyKawaii, she co-runs The Kitsunés, the creative partnership behind her visual work.

Majestic Phoenix brings together composer and multi-instrumentalist Aaron McLean and producer and audio engineer Kent “Von” Hertzog, whose friendship and creative partnership began at the Art Institute of Philadelphia in 1999. Reuniting decades later, the American cinematic electropop duo returned to musical ideas left unfinished during their college years. Those recovered recordings, alongside new material, became their debut EP, Manifest, released in October 2025. McLean writes, performs, and produces the music, while Hertzog contributes co-production, mixing, and mastering at The Social Club, drawing on his background in audio engineering and hip-hop production. Their music combines electronic textures from earlier eras with contemporary arrangements, balancing melodic detail with atmosphere and emotional expression. Friendship, fate, and creative renewal inform the project, with subsequent releases inviting vocal collaborators into the partnership. Their association with The Kitsunés also extends to the duo’s artwork and visual identity.

items.title: Violet Nox Let the Flowers Rule the Planet in their Surreal Video for “Spectre,” Black Snow on Christmas Remix
items.summary: Somewhere between the primordial swamp and the outer reaches of the cosmos, Violet Nox have discovered a rather splendid place to lose your mind. Their new remix of Spectre, courtesy of… The post Violet Nox Let the Flowers Rule the Planet in their Surreal Vide
items.fullText:
Somewhere between the primordial swamp and the outer reaches of the cosmos, Violet Nox have discovered a rather splendid place to lose your mind. Their new remix of Spectre, courtesy of German electronic experimentalist Chris Wirrwitz (Black Snow on Christmas), sends the Boston outfit’s extraterrestrial excursions hurtling through an electronic wilderness where flowers dance, planets collide, and the machinery of existence appears to have developed a considerable appetite for psychedelics.

Originally released on Violet Nox’s October 2025 album Silvae through Somewherecold Records, Spectre already possessed the sort of cosmic curiosity that could send a reasonably sober person searching the heavens for intelligent life. Wirrwitz, who has spent three decades exploring everything from experimental rock to modular synthesis, takes those foundations and sets the controls for a rather more turbulent destination.

The synthesizers roll forward in great undulating waves, their melodic contours continually shifting beneath rhythms that seem to have acquired minds of their own. Dorsey’s extraordinary vocals rise through the electronic undergrowth, invoking the spectral grandeur of Dead Can Dance while carrying an unmistakable sense of earthly vulnerability. Every new layer introduces another possibility, another strange passage through a composition that seems perpetually on the verge of swallowing its own coordinates. Beneath the kaleidoscopic mischief runs a fascinating tension between organic life and technological invention.

And then comes Allison Tanenhaus’s magnificent music video, a gloriously deranged excursion into the sort of science-fiction paradise that might have resulted if Fantastic Planet, vintage anime, and a particularly ambitious planetarium exhibition had somehow reproduced. Wirrwitz’s synthesizers advance through the composition with restless determination, while Tanenhaus gives their movements physical form through rotating structures, celestial bodies, and constantly transforming landscapes.

Circles spin across impossible horizons. Prismatic light fractures into geometric formations, constellations drift through vast expanses of darkness, and alien vegetation sways with the peculiar enthusiasm of organisms that have discovered music for the first time. The imagery continually mutates, suggesting an ecosystem where biology and mathematics have entered into some deliciously questionable arrangement.

Those purple flowers deserve special attention. Their theatrical movements recall the botanical chorus of Disney’s version of Alice in Wonderland, particularly All in the Golden Afternoon, although Tanenhaus has transported these cheerful little exhibitionists into territory where Lewis Carroll might have benefited from a spacecraft and a substantial supply of tranquilizers.

Additional production from Andrew Abrahamson and Dez DeCarlo of Violet Nox, with mastering by Abrahamson, completes an excursion into electronic psychedelia that feels wonderfully untethered from ordinary geography.
