items.title: Angelzoom releases new single ‘Borrowed Light’
items.summary: German darkwave project Angelzoom released the single "Borrowed Light" on November 6, ahead of a fourth studio album due in mid-2027.
items.fullText:
German darkwave project Angelzoom released the single “Borrowed Light” on Bandcamp on November 6. The track follows the single “Grey Devotion” and is the first single from Angelzoom’s planned fourth studio album, due in mid-2027.

Angelzoom is the project of German singer Claudia Uhle. “Borrowed Light” was written by Uhle and Bernd Wendlandt, with Uhle on vocals and piano and Wendlandt on keyboards and programming; Wendlandt also produced the track. An official video is set to premiere on YouTube on November 13.

“Borrowed Light” is available to stream and download on Bandcamp.

About Angelzoom

Angelzoom is the atmospheric darkwave project of German singer Claudia Uhle, combining electronic textures with emotionally driven songwriting. The project released its self-titled debut album in 2004, followed by “Nothing Is Infinite” in 2010. Angelzoom continued with the single “Grey Devotion” before “Borrowed Light,” released November 6, 2026, which points toward Angelzoom’s fourth studio album, planned for mid-2027.

items.title: Blac Kolor and Bedless Bones announce collaborative album ‘Mimetic Desire’
items.summary: Blac Kolor's Hendrick Grothe and Bedless Bones' Kadri Sammel are working on a joint album, "Mimetic Desire," tentatively due in summer 2027 with live shows.
items.fullText:
Blac Kolor, the project of German producer Hendrick Grothe, and Bedless Bones, the project of Estonian artist Kadri Sammel, are working on a full-length collaborative album titled “Mimetic Desire.” The record is tentatively expected in summer 2027 and will be accompanied by live performances, the two artists told Side-Line exclusively.

Grothe produces industrial electronics, EBM, IDM, techno and experimental sound design, while Sammel moves between darkwave, EBM, experimental electronics and atmospheric songwriting. Blac Kolor previously remixed Bedless Bones’ track “Revelations” for the expanded edition of her debut album “Sublime Malaise,” but “Mimetic Desire” is their first full album together.

No plan at the start

Speaking to Side-Line, Grothe said the collaboration began without any intention of making a full record. “There was no big masterplan in the first place. I just had a vague idea, that it could be interesting to join forces.”

He had already been working on new material when he began wondering what Sammel’s voice could bring to it. “I asked her and she was just on fire collaborating. After the first few exchanged bits we realized, that we hold something very special in our hands here. Everything is sounding very unique.”

Sammel described how what started as a guest appearance grew into a full album. “Hendrick pretty much summed it up. He approached me with his new material, which was instantly very inspiring. I found it difficult to pick one song, and he didn’t want to pick it for me either, so I tried some vocals for several songs, and he ended up liking them all, so I did more.”

“I expected him to use some samples or lines for a single track, but the snowball somehow got rolling,” she added.

A title from René Girard

The album’s title refers to mimetic desire, a concept developed by French philosopher and literary theorist René Girard describing how human desires are shaped through imitation of others. Sammel confirmed the concept is Grothe’s own: “The music and the concept of René Girard’s mimetic desire are all Hendrick’s.” How he will develop the idea musically and lyrically has not been detailed yet.

Grothe confirmed the partnership will extend to the stage, with plans to bring “Mimetic Desire” to live audiences. No concert dates or venues have been announced. Further details on the album’s release date, tracklist and live presentation are expected to follow.

About Blac Kolor

Blac Kolor is the electronic music project of German producer Hendrick Grothe, combining industrial electronics, EBM, IDM, techno and experimental sound design. Since his debut album “Wide Noise” in 2014, Grothe has built an approach built on intricate rhythmic programming, distorted electronic textures and powerful basslines, followed by “Born in Ruins” (2016), “Awakening” (2018) and “Times of Upheaval” (2021). His 2023 album “Weltenbrand,” released through Ant-Zen, explored environmental destruction and conflict with guest vocalists including Panternoise, Jennifer Touch, XTR HUMAN and Donis. Its follow-up, “Arca” (2025, also Ant-Zen), used the biblical plagues as a framework for examining contemporary human behaviour. Side-Line interviewed Grothe about his work in April 2026.

About Bedless Bones

Bedless Bones is the solo project of Kadri Sammel, an Estonian vocalist, producer, multi-instrumentalist and interdisciplinary artist based in Tallinn, with a background in choral singing, cultural theory, audiovisual media and photography. Her debut album “Sublime Malaise” (2019) combined melancholic synthesizers, industrial rhythms and introspective songwriting, and was later expanded and reissued internationally through Metropolis Records. “Bending the Iron Bough” (2021) added acoustic instruments, folk influences and mythological references, and her third album, “Mire of Mercury” (2023, Metropolis Records), continued that direction with a music video for the track “Solar Animus.” Sammel is also a member of the Estonian avant-garde industrial group Forgotten Sunrise, the vocalist of UK-Estonian project Deathsomnia, and performs as DJ Dirt Vessel within Tallinn’s Beats From The Vault scene. The “Mimetic Desire” collaboration with Blac Kolor is her first full-length team-up with another artist.

items.title: Tobias Bernstrup releases single ‘Love Machines’
items.summary: Swedish artist Tobias Bernstrup releases the single "Love Machines," mastered by Doruk Ozturkcan, streaming now on Bandcamp ahead of a vinyl compilation.
items.fullText:
Swedish artist Tobias Bernstrup released the single “Love Machines” on Bandcamp on November 6, 2026. Doruk Ozturkcan of She Past Away mastered the track, which Bernstrup also plans to include on the upcoming vinyl compilation “Fred Ventura Presents Italo International.”

An Italo-synth single about human and machine

Bernstrup wrote and performs “Love Machines” as commentary on the growing interaction between humans and computers, and on artificial intelligence replacing parts of what previously defined human individuality. He described the track as “rawer, more minimal and more analogously stripped down than usual.” Bernstrup also handled the single’s sleeve photo and graphic design. Bandcamp tags the track as electronic, Italo disco, synthpop and synthwave.

“Love Machines” is set to appear on “Fred Ventura Presents Italo International,” an upcoming vinyl compilation of modern Italo disco and electronic dance music. “Love Machines” is available to stream and download on Bandcamp.

About Tobias Bernstrup

Tobias Bernstrup is a Swedish artist and musician, born July 17, 1970, in Gothenburg. He studied at the Royal College University of Fine Arts in Stockholm from 1993 to 1998, earning an MFA, and later spent time at the International Studio & Curatorial Program in New York from 2002 to 2003. At the Royal College he met artist Palle Torsson, and the two collaborated as Museum Meltdown from 1995 to 1999, showing at Arken in Copenhagen, the Contemporary Art Centre in Vilnius and Moderna Museet in Stockholm.

Bernstrup has worked across video, interactive media, live performance and electronic music, developing a stage persona and digital avatar and composing electronic music for Swedish video artist Annika Larsson. His solo exhibitions include “Almost Human” (2010, Gothenburg Art Museum and Andréhn-Schiptjenko, Stockholm), “Killing Spree” (2005-2006, Galleri Niklas Belenius, Stockholm), “South Of Heaven” (2014-2017, shown in Stockholm, Uddevalla and Barcelona) and “Night In The Science Zone” (Andréhn-Schiptjenko, Stockholm, 2020). His work is represented in the collections of Moderna Museet and FRAC Champagne-Ardenne.

Bernstrup, who discussed his approach to music-making in a prior Side-Line interview, has released music through Wierd Records, Falco Invernale Records, Black Leather Records, Mannequin Records, Other Voices Records, DiscoModernism and Tonight Records, and more recently through Nadanna Records, which issued his albums “Technophobic” (2018) and “Petrichor” (2021) and the single “Shadow Dancer” (2025). “Love Machines” follows that run of Nadanna-era releases and continues Bernstrup’s Italo disco and synth-driven sound ahead of his appearance on “Fred Ventura Presents Italo International.”

items.title: New Order announces March 2027 U.S. tour dates
items.summary: New Order announces a seven-date March 2027 U.S. tour with Future Islands, days ahead of the band's Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction with Joy Division.
items.fullText:
New Order has announced its first U.S. dates of 2027, a seven-show run opening March 5 at Austin’s Moody Center and closing with two nights at the Fillmore Miami Beach on March 20 and 21. Future Islands join the Manchester band for all three Texas dates, with artist presale opening November 10 and general tickets on sale November 13.

Tour dates for New Order

  • March 5, Austin, TX, Moody Center (with Future Islands and Zachery Allan Starkey)
  • March 7, Fort Worth, TX, Ariat Arena (with Future Islands, Zachery Allan Starkey and DJ TinTin)
  • March 10, Houston, TX, Toyota Center (with Future Islands)
  • March 13, New Orleans, LA, The Fillmore New Orleans (with Zachery Allan Starkey)
  • March 16, Nashville, TN, The Truth (with Zachery Allan Starkey)
  • March 20, Miami Beach, FL, The Fillmore Miami Beach at Jackie Gleason Theater (with DJ Arthur Baker)
  • March 21, Miami Beach, FL, The Fillmore Miami Beach at Jackie Gleason Theater (with DJ Arthur Baker)

Arthur Baker, who co-produced New Order’s 1983 single “Confusion” with the band, will DJ both Miami Beach shows. Before the U.S. dates, New Order plays six shows across Brazil, Chile, Argentina, Peru and Colombia, starting November 23 in São Paulo and wrapping December 9 in Bogotá.

Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction

The U.S. tour announcement arrives five days before Joy Division and New Order enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame together, at a ceremony set for November 14, 2026, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. The Hall inducts Ian Curtis, Peter Hook, Stephen Morris, Bernard Sumner and Gillian Gilbert, who formed New Order after Curtis’s 1980 death and brought Gilbert into the band shortly after. It is the pairing’s third nomination, following earlier ballots in 2023 and 2025. The recorded ceremony airs on ABC on December 8, then streams on Disney+ and Hulu the following day.

New Order will play the March dates with touring musicians filling in for drummer Stephen Morris and keyboardist and guitarist Gillian Gilbert, who said in June they would step away from touring for the foreseeable future. Gilbert later clarified in a statement that she, not Morris, is undergoing cancer treatment: “It is in fact me, who like many other people, is living with cancer,” she wrote, thanking fans for their support and asking for privacy during treatment.

The induction follows a year of catalogue activity for both bands. New Order remastered and expanded “(The Best Of) New Order” and “(The Rest Of) New Order,” following 2026’s “Brotherhood” anniversary, while Joy Division’s “Eternal (Live)” box set collects 16 performances, including a Birmingham show where the band played “Ceremony” live for the only time; New Order made the song their debut single the following year.

About New Order

New Order formed in Manchester in 1980, when guitarist Bernard Sumner, bassist Peter Hook and drummer Stephen Morris regrouped following the death of Joy Division singer Ian Curtis and brought in Gillian Gilbert on keyboards and guitar. The band’s catalogue moved from the post-punk of Joy Division into electronic dance music on records including “Movement,” “Power, Corruption & Lies” and “Technique,” with singles such as “Blue Monday” and “Confusion,” the latter co-produced with Arthur Baker. Hook left the band in 2007. New Order and Joy Division enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame together on November 14, 2026, and New Order tours the U.S. in March 2027 with Future Islands.

items.title: Rosa Damask releases new single ‘Crygirl’, shares video
items.summary: Berlin artist Rosa Damask releases the single "Crygirl" and a video directed by Andrii Kaplia, following her post-punk album "Adore You."
items.fullText:
Berlin artist Rosa Damask released the single “Crygirl” on Bandcamp, with a video directed by Andrii Kaplia. Rosa Damask is the solo project of Nastia Reigel, a Berlin-based musician and producer.

A heavy, bass-led single

“Crygirl” is built around a throbbing bass line and heavy drums, with a thick guitar riff leading into the chorus and sighing synth pads underneath. Reigel’s vocal stays close to the microphone throughout, singing about losing her bearings and feeling estranged from people who still see her as the person she used to be. Kaplia’s video surrounds Reigel with burgundy carpets, patterned wallpaper and gilt mirrors, following her through a series of rooms in a black suit as her reflection multiplies around her.

“Crygirl” is available to stream and order on Bandcamp.

About Rosa Damask

Rosa Damask is the solo project of Nastia Reigel, a Berlin-based musician and producer who came up in St. Petersburg’s techno scene, where she founded the queer club night Грань (Grahn’) in 2018. She has also composed music for art-house films. Reigel appeared on Vatican Shadow‘s Berghain Mix 09 before releasing music through his Hospital Productions label, and recordings she made between 2018 and 2020 became the basis of her 2021 release “Memorials” on DKA. She moved from the largely electronic approach of that record into guitar-led post-punk on “Adore You,” her album for Downwards Records, whose track “Bored” was used in Versace’s Fall/Winter 2025 runway show in Milan. Kaplia, who directed “Adore You”‘s title-track video and has filmed Reigel’s live performances at Morphine Raum and Silent Space, also made the video for “Crygirl,” her latest single.

items.title: Amulet releases ‘I am the Dark’, first single from new album ‘The Dark’
items.summary: Amulet releases "I am the Dark," the first single from third album "The Dark," produced by Christopher Hall of Stabbing Westward, with a new video.
items.fullText:
Washington, D.C. gothic rock band Amulet released “I am the Dark” on November 5, 2026, through Distortion Productions. The track is the first single from the band’s third studio album, “The Dark,” due April 30, 2027, and opens a planned six-single campaign ahead of it. Christopher Hall of Stabbing Westward produced the single, which also arrives in a Stabbing Westward remix.

Gothic rock, darkwave and industrial electronics

“I am the Dark” opens on an organ melody before a deep bassline and drums set the track in motion, with thick gothic rock guitars and an organ flourish running beneath singer Stephanie Stryker’s lead vocal. Principal songwriter and multi-instrumentalist MJ Phoenix wrote the music; guitarist Bob Carr and drummer Billy Holler complete the band’s live lineup. Lyrically, the song gives depression and fear a vampiric shape, with images of burial and waking death standing in for the exhaustion of getting through an ordinary day.

A Stabbing Westward remix of “I am the Dark” recasts the song’s gothic rock instrumentation with industrial beats and synthesizers. Bandcamp pre-orders for both versions opened November 6, 2026, ahead of a wider release across streaming platforms on November 13, 2026.

‘I am the Dark’ video

Filmed by Illumination Media at Crescendo Studios and edited and styled by Stryker, the video places the band in a stark, near-monochrome studio setting, cutting between full-band shots and close views of Stryker in a crowned, corseted costume. Custom garments came from Angel’s House of Design Co., with her choker supplied by Cult of Asmodeus.

“I am the Dark” is available digitally on Bandcamp, with the album “The Dark” following on digital, CD and vinyl formats.

About Amulet

Amulet is a Washington, D.C. gothic rock band led by singer Stephanie Stryker and songwriter and multi-instrumentalist MJ Phoenix, joined live by guitarist Bob Carr and drummer Billy Holler. The band released its debut single “When Winter Comes” in December 2023 and signed to Distortion Productions in 2022. Amulet’s catalogue includes the 2024 album “Katharsis” and the 2025 remix EP “Purification,” which featured reworks by Interface and Tragic Impulse. “The Dark,” the band’s third album, continues its exploration of the supernatural as a language for emotional experience, opening with “I am the Dark” and its Christopher Hall-produced Stabbing Westward remix.

items.title: Nightcrawler releases Chernobyl-inspired concept album ‘Uranium 235’
items.summary: Nightcrawler releases concept album "Uranium 235," inspired by Chernobyl, on Bandcamp and CD, with a new "System Lies" video.
items.fullText:
Spanish electronic music producer Nightcrawler released the concept album “Uranium 235” on November 5, 2026, on his own label Nightcrawler Music. The nine-track record is built around the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster and is available as a digital album and on CD in a 4-panel digipack, alongside a limited box edition of ten copies.

A concept album built around Chernobyl

“Uranium 235” follows a narrative arc from the first signs of the disaster to its aftermath, structured to be heard from beginning to end rather than as individual tracks. The album moves through EBM, electro and dark techno rhythms, with industrial textures and more experimental passages marking its tenser passages. Nightcrawler produced, mixed and mastered the album himself at NC Sound Studio, his own studio, and the cover design is by George Gold Design, which also created the artwork for the 2025 Nightcrawler and Spammerheads collaboration “Ghostless.”

‘Uranium 235’ tracklisting

  1. “Radiation”
  2. “Pripyat 1986”
  3. “System Lies” (feat. Carmilla Sioux)
  4. “Dosimeter”
  5. “Reactor 4”
  6. “Phase”
  7. “U-235”
  8. “Protocol AZ-5” (feat. Nghtly)
  9. “Evacuation”

Carmilla Sioux contributes to the production of “System Lies,” and Italian producer Nghtly collaborates on “Protocol AZ-5.”

‘System Lies’ video, and the album’s dystopian universe

Nightcrawler directed a new music video for “System Lies,” made with generative video techniques and centered on the control and manipulation of information. It is the second video from the album, following “Reactor 4,” which Side-Line covered when it preceded “Uranium 235” as the album’s lead single in September 2026. That video explores a dystopian post-nuclear city, moving from inside a power plant to its surrounding areas; “Uranium 235” places both videos, and all nine tracks, within the same imagined aftermath of the disaster.

“Uranium 235” is available to stream and download on Bandcamp and other digital platforms.

About Nightcrawler

Nightcrawler is a Spanish electronic music project active since 2011, working at the intersection of horror and sci-fi film scoring and darker electronic rhythms. The project’s catalogue includes the “Strange Shadows” EP and releases such as “Visionary” and “Metropolis,” and its April 2025 collaboration with Valencia-based EBM duo Spammerheads, “Ghostless.” “Uranium 235” is Nightcrawler’s first full concept album, following “Reactor 4” as its lead single.

items.title: Erasure share Ladytron remix of ‘Wings Of Love’, announce CD single
items.summary: Erasure release a Ladytron remix of "Wings Of Love," confirm a five-track CD single for December 15 on Mute, and report 100,000 tour tickets sold.
items.fullText:
English synth-pop duo Erasure released a remix of their single “Wings Of Love” by Ladytron on November 10, 2026, and confirmed a five-track CD single of the song for December 15 on Mute. The remix is the second piece of music drawn from Erasure’s forthcoming album “Radio!! Radio!!,” due March 12, 2027, and arrives alongside an update on the duo’s 2027 arena tour, which has now sold 100,000 tickets.

Ladytron’s remix of ‘Wings Of Love’

Ladytron‘s remix of “Wings Of Love” is available to stream and download across digital platforms. An official visualiser, built around the robot figure “Dolly” from the “Radio!! Radio!!” cover art, is streaming on YouTube. Ladytron appear as special guests on Erasure’s 2027 UK arena dates, and previously released a DJ Slow rework of “We Never Went Away” in 2024. Erasure has a history of commissioning remixes of its own singles, including a 2017 remix of “Love You To The Sky”.

‘Wings Of Love’ CD single, out December 15

Erasure will release “Wings Of Love” as a five-track CD single on December 15, the first in a planned series of CD singles from the “Radio!! Radio!!” album campaign. The CD includes two tracks exclusive to the format: an extended mix by producer Gareth Jones and a remix by Mute labelmate Miss Grit.

“Wings Of Love” CD single tracklisting: – “Wings Of Love” – “Wings Of Love” (Gareth Jones Extended Angel Mix) – “Wings Of Love” (Ladytron Remix) – “Wings Of Love” (Miss Grit Remix) – “Wings Of Love” (Radio Mix)

The single is aimed at members of the Erasure Information Service and will be sold through Lexer Music and Mute Bank, which ships to the UK, EU and North America. It will not be available from other retailers.

Radio!! Radio!! tour: 100,000 tickets sold, four dates sold out

Erasure reported that 100,000 tickets have been sold for the 2027 “Radio!! Radio!!” tour of the UK and Europe, which runs from April 25 to May 28 with Ladytron as special guests on the UK and Ireland dates. The Cardiff opening night at Utilita Arena on April 25, both Leipzig shows at Haus Auensee on May 18 and May 19, and the Berlin date at Uber Eats Music Hall on May 24 are now sold out. Side-Line previously reported the full “Radio!! Radio!!” album, tracklisting and tour details when they were announced in September 2026.

About Erasure

Erasure are the English synth-pop duo of vocalist Andy Bell and instrumentalist Vince Clarke, formed in London in 1985 and signed to Mute Records. The duo marked 40 years since their 1986 debut album, “Wonderland,” in 2026. “Radio!! Radio!!,” their 20th studio album, is due March 12, 2027, and follows 2022’s “Day-Glo (Based on a True Story).” Side-Line’s earlier coverage has the duo’s recent reissue campaigns, solo projects and the album and tour announcement in full.

items.title: Grauzone Festival 2027: The Art of Staying Unclassifiable
items.summary: Grauzone Festival returns to The Hague on 12-14 February 2027 with Ladytron, She Past Away, Mareux, Cold Cave, Au Pairs, Iceage and Martin Dupont.
items.fullText:
There is a particular danger that comes with the growing popularity of underground music: the aesthetics that once represented artistic independence can gradually become a collection of recognisable sounds, familiar silhouettes and carefully maintained expectations. The more established a scene becomes, the easier it is to confuse loyalty to its history with the obligation to keep repeating it. Grauzone Festival has spent more than a decade exploring a different possibility, bringing together musicians whose work is connected by curiosity and experimentation rather than by a strict definition of what dark or alternative music should sound like.

Returning to The Hague, Netherlands, from February 12 to 14, 2027, Grauzone will once again transform the city centre into a meeting place for post-punk, darkwave, experimental electronics, industrial music, art and performance. The announced programme is exceptionally extensive, combining artists whose careers reach back to the origins of post-punk with contemporary musicians exploring the boundaries of electronic composition, guitar music and underground culture.

The festival was founded in 2013 by Natasja Alers and Marc Emmerik, initially taking place at Amsterdam’s Melkweg before moving to The Hague. Its beginnings were rooted in a straightforward frustration: many of the musicians they admired rarely performed in the Netherlands, while the existing concert landscape offered relatively few opportunities to bring different strands of underground culture together.

When I spoke with Natasja and Marc in 2024, Natasja recalled the influence of Berlin’s post-punk and darkwave scene during her studies at the Weissensee Academy of Art. After returning to the Netherlands, she began organising performances by artists including Lebanon Hanover and Linea Aspera, eventually developing the idea of a festival with Marc. Even the name Grauzone emerged from that desire to create a space between established categories. The intention was to accommodate music, visual art, film and performance within a shared cultural environment, without treating any one discipline as secondary.

Marc explained that their programming involved constant research, conversations and a sometimes complicated process of combining established performers with artists representing newer developments. That philosophy remains apparent in the 2027 lineup, where historically important names appear alongside projects that are still developing their artistic identities.

Grauzone 2027: Ladytron, She Past Away, Mareux and Martin Dupont

Among the major names announced are Ladytron, marking the group’s return to the Netherlands after almost twenty years. The British electronic group helped shape the early-2000s relationship between synthpop, electroclash and darker alternative music, developing a distinctive balance of melodic precision, detached vocal delivery and sharp electronic arrangements. Songs such as “Seventeen” and “Destroy Everything You Touch” remain important reference points, while their 2026 album “Paradises” demonstrates that the group’s artistic trajectory extends well beyond the period with which they are most frequently associated.

The Turkish duo She Past Away represent another influential development in contemporary darkwave. Their austere guitar lines, insistent bass patterns, sombre Turkish-language vocals and unmistakable rhythmic character have attracted an international following while retaining a sound rooted in post-punk’s more introspective traditions. Alongside them, Mareux brings a more sensual approach to electronic melancholy, combining darkwave atmospheres with synthpop melodies and an immediate appeal to the dancefloor. His success with “The Perfect Girl” introduced his music to a much broader audience, although his catalogue reveals a more varied relationship with electronic pop.

For listeners interested in the genre’s earlier history, Martin Dupont are among the programme’s most intriguing names. Emerging from Marseille’s experimental scene in the early 1980s, the French group developed an unusual combination of minimal electronics, saxophone, unconventional arrangements and highly individual vocal expression. Their work occupied a territory that never fitted comfortably into the conventional categories of synthpop or post-punk, which makes their presence at Grauzone especially appropriate.

Another important historical connection comes through Au Pairs, the influential Birmingham post-punk group led by Lesley Woods. Their 1981 album “Playing With A Different Sex” remains a striking example of how political and feminist perspectives could be articulated through rhythmically inventive music drawing on punk, funk and experimental rock. The revived lineup, featuring musicians associated with Big Joanie, Pere Ubu and the Thurston Moore Group, brings that legacy into a contemporary context.

Danish band Iceage add another dimension to the programme, having developed from the urgency of their early punk recordings towards more elaborate songwriting incorporating art rock and darker, more atmospheric arrangements. Their inclusion connects Grauzone’s electronic and post-punk interests with a more volatile tradition of guitar-driven experimentation.

Cold Cave to perform ‘Cremations’ in Europe for the first time

One of the festival’s notable announcements concerns Cold Cave, who will present a special solo performance of “Cremations.” Rather than another concert devoted to the project’s better-known synthpop material, founder Wes Eisold will revisit the earliest Cold Cave recordings, collected under that title in 2009. The material documents a period when his music occupied a rawer territory between industrial electronics, noise, shoegaze and primitive synth composition, before the project developed its more recognisable melodic character.

Following a small number of performances in the United States, Grauzone will host the first European presentation of this special “Cremations” set. For an audience familiar primarily with Cold Cave’s later work, it offers an opportunity to encounter the project’s formative experiments and the artistic decisions that eventually guided its evolution.

Electronic and punk programme

The electronic programme is equally substantial. French producer The Hacker, one of the central figures in the development of electroclash and contemporary electro, will perform with Swedish musician Rein. Their collaborative album “We Come Alive,” released in 2026, brings together elements of EBM, darkwave and electro, combining The Hacker’s formidable command of electronic rhythm with Rein’s forceful vocal presence and interest in the physical energy of body music.

Curses, meanwhile, will appear with a full live band, expanding the guitar-driven, romantic and occasionally theatrical qualities of his dark electronic compositions. Dina Summer, the Berlin-based collaboration between Local Suicide and Kalipo, bring their own combination of electroclash, Italo-disco and new wave. Their recent mini-album “Children Of The Night” explores a darker musical palette, incorporating the influence of gothic culture into the trio’s characteristic understanding of electronic songwriting and club rhythms.

Australian producer Buzz Kull approaches electronic music from a different angle, bringing coldwave melodies, mechanical percussion and emotionally distant vocals into arrangements that are both hypnotic and highly danceable. Rosa Anschütz occupies a more atmospheric territory, moving between avant-pop, electronics and introspective songwriting, while Laura Krieg brings a sharper, politically conscious approach to synth-punk and minimal electronic composition.

The lineup also features Unhuman & Petra Flurr, whose aggressive electronic performances draw on the physical intensity of EBM, industrial techno and punk. Ghost Cop, Mothermary, Grenzkontrolle, Night In Athens, Mercy Girl, Aux Animaux and Josephine Olivia extend the programme across different expressions of dark electronics, contemporary goth and post-punk. Together with Istanbul-based Jakuzi, whose Turkish-language synthpop has acquired a distinctive international identity, and Ductape, who approach darkwave through a combination of melancholic melodies and forceful rhythms, they demonstrate how widely these musical influences have travelled.

There is also considerable emphasis on artists whose work challenges the idea that an underground festival must remain within the familiar boundaries of guitars, synthesizers and drum machines.

American composer Kelly Moran, for instance, brings the possibilities of the prepared piano into the programme. Her music explores resonance, repetition and the transformation of acoustic sound through electronic processes, creating elaborate compositions whose shimmering textures often conceal remarkable structural complexity.

Marissa Nadler offers another form of intimacy. Her compositions inhabit the territory between dark folk, gothic Americana, ambient music and dreamlike songwriting, with her unmistakable voice carrying narratives built from memory, loss and psychological ambiguity. Canadian musician Ora Cogan similarly moves between folk, psychedelic pop and gothic country, while approaching those traditions through her own distinctive vocal and compositional sensibility.

The experimental interests continue with Annie-Claude Deschênes, known for her work with Duchess Says, whose solo project combines synth-punk, minimal electronics and performance art. Zoe Heselton draws on folk, blues, flamenco and free jazz, creating an approach to songwriting that resists easy classification. Holy Motors, from Tallinn, bring a more dreamlike guitar atmosphere, with their slow-moving arrangements and spacious melodies offering another contrast to the electronic intensity.

Grauzone’s guitar-oriented programme is notable for its diversity. American group The Velveteers, making their Dutch debut, combine grunge, glam and punk with a powerful two-drummer setup, while New Zealand duo Earth Tongue explore heavy psychedelic rock through fuzzy guitars and forceful rhythmic arrangements. Cardiel, from Mexico, combine stoner rock, psychedelia, grunge and dub within a compact guitar-and-drums format.

The return of punk’s more confrontational traditions can be heard in Canadian group Béton Armé, whose French-language Oi! draws on political and working-class themes, and in the abrasive art-rock of American band Dana. Tube Alloys, Primitive Ring, Bande À Part, Saint Just, Beaks, Body Shop and The Woman further expand the guitar, electronic and post-punk spectrum, each approaching the relationship between rhythmic experimentation and alternative songwriting from a different direction.

The programme also includes Aurat, whose industrial electro-punk combines danceable electronic structures with Urdu-language vocals, and Theo Vandenhoff, whose appearance marks an important European opportunity for the Canadian artist. Villanelle, Zonbi, Katie Bitchcoin, Mye_Taai, She Can’t Afford Mascara and several additional artists illustrate the organisers’ continuing commitment to less predictable bookings and emerging underground talent.

Beyond the live performances, the festival’s late-night programme will feature Phase Fatale, presenting a special wave-oriented set, alongside Intergalactic Gary, Ofra and Esther Dune. Their different approaches to electronic music, ranging from obscure Italo-disco and electro to industrial rhythms and darkwave, should provide a complementary perspective on many of the sounds explored during the concerts.

GRAUKUNST: visual art, film and performance

Yet Grauzone’s identity has never depended exclusively on its musical programme. The festival’s expansion into The Hague allowed its founders to develop the interdisciplinary ambitions that had been present from the beginning. Rather than confining underground culture to a single venue, the event has gradually established connections with galleries, cinemas and other spaces throughout the city.

The GRAUKUNST exhibitions, film screenings, discussions and performance programme form a core part of that identity, encouraging connections between disciplines that often share artistic concerns but rarely receive equal attention at music festivals. Further details of the 2027 visual art, film and performance programme are still expected, alongside additional artist announcements.

During our earlier conversation, Natasja and Marc also emphasised the importance of the people who attend Grauzone. They described an audience drawn from different countries and cultural backgrounds, united less by adherence to a particular subculture than by openness, musical curiosity and the freedom to express individual identities.

The 2027 programme reflects that philosophy with considerable clarity. Ladytron and Martin Dupont represent different chapters of electronic music’s history; Cold Cave return to an earlier, noisier incarnation; Kelly Moran and Marissa Nadler open the programme towards entirely different acoustic and compositional possibilities. Around them, younger artists reinterpret familiar influences through their own cultural experiences, while the punk and experimental performers prevent the festival’s darker aesthetic from becoming too comfortable.

The most persuasive aspect of Grauzone is therefore not simply the number of important names on its poster, impressive though they are. It is the organisers’ willingness to place those names in contexts that encourage discovery, to connect the past with developing artistic ideas and to treat underground culture as something continually being created rather than a historical period to be faithfully reconstructed.

  • Location: The Hague, Netherlands
  • Tickets: early bird and regular weekend passes are sold out; late weekend tickets, including a young-persons rate (up to 25 years), remain available through the official festival website
  • Website: Grauzone Festival

items.title: Golden Apes interview: ‘The Sun Rises Only and Solely from the Dark’
items.summary: Peer Lebrecht of Golden Apes talks to Side-Line about light, darkness and physical imagery on "The Sun Came Up Tremendously," out via Icy Cold Records.
items.fullText:
There is a particular quality to the music of Golden Apes that makes it difficult to confine within the familiar vocabulary of gothic rock and post-punk. Melancholy, darkness and longing are certainly present, but they are rarely straightforward emotions. They shift, contradict one another and sometimes reveal entirely different meanings depending on the words, the arrangements or the smallest change in atmosphere. There is poetry in this ambiguity, and considerable musical sensitivity in the way the band allows it to unfold.

With their twelfth studio album, “The Sun Came Up Tremendously”, released on September 18, 2026, through Icy Cold Records, the Berlin musicians continue developing an artistic language that has become unmistakably their own. Peer Lebrecht’s resonant voice, the carefully layered guitar arrangements and the band’s characteristic interplay between melodic weight and atmospheric space form the foundation of a record whose beauty is inseparable from its emotional complexity.

I recently spoke with Peer Lebrecht for Side-Line about the new album and the artistic sensibility that continues to define Golden Apes.

Golden Apes interview

Karo: “The Sun Came Up Tremendously” feels very recognisably Golden Apes, but not in the sense of repeating an old formula. After twelve albums, how do you distinguish between continuity and self-imitation? At what point does a characteristic sound become an artistic language you can still expand rather than a set of habits you have to escape?

Peer: If you want me to be quite honest – I don’t distinguish at all.

I don’t even feel the need to think about things written back then when I deal with something new. I’m someone who easily closes a chapter when I reach the final full stop, and there are, honestly, Apes albums I haven’t listened to since they were released. I just don’t feel the need. It may sound strange, but the moment the music is out, it has left my personal space, the sphere of intimacy.

While working on an album, everything is somehow entwined with the time in which it was created – the music, the words, the feelings – conditional snapshots. And as time moves on, so do certain conditions, perceptions, thoughts, impressions… Listening to old songs feels a bit like reading the diary of a person you barely know. And maybe it’s exactly that. Sure, there are some memories you share and images that trigger your cortex, but sensations have shifted, points of view have changed… fragments of memories of a feeling.

I don’t deny that there might be colours and patterns that turn up now and then throughout the canon. In the end, it’s still the same head, but I don’t care because then they seem to be part of my musical language, my sonic vocabulary.

For me, the blank page is always set in the here and now. The current state is the developer – no knotted striving for innovation, no expectations, no genre or stylistic constraints. If I like an idea, I go with it, and there’s no no-go as long as your curiosity is hungry.

Karo: Light appears throughout the album, but it is never simply positive. In “The Light (Inside Us),” it is something already present within us; in “Radiation,” it becomes almost overwhelming; and in “Helion,” it arrives after wounds, shadows and exhaustion. Were you interested in destabilising the usual opposition between light as salvation and darkness as danger?

Peer: Maybe I was never really convinced of this strict opposite-things theory.

Yes, at first glance, light has quite a solid and positive reputation, but there’s something lurking in the shadows. (Sorry, I had to.)

I’ve always been in awe of light’s ability to reveal things. When lightning strikes, a lamp suddenly switched on in a dark room, illumination in your head… the exposure of things we sometimes never wanted to see. Truths, failures, atrocities… yourself…

Don’t get me wrong – I like light. With all its spectral colours, its grandeur and sense of fairness, but it’s merciless. It can blind you, it can hurt you, lead you astray and cast away the shadows, the shelters…

Maybe it’s a question of wavelength or just the angle of incidence, but for me, light has never been solely redeeming. “Fiat Lux” is not necessarily a consolation…

Karo: The title phrase appears in “Helion,” roughly in the middle of the record rather than at its conclusion. That changes how I read the album because the sunrise is followed by “Where the River Ran,” “Evelyn,” “Radiation,” “City Walls” and finally “Dreams (Gone By).” Was it important that illumination should occur inside the story rather than resolve it?

Peer: As you already mentioned – the sun and its light as a symbol or metaphor might have different interpretations within the individual songs and lyrics. It is, as so often, a question of context.

Let’s take the opener “Farewell.” Here, the sunrise is a measure of time, a kind of countdown, a trigger. In “Helion,” it serves more as a harbinger, an announcement of an unshakeable truth. “Milk & Poison” sees it blinding and hurting as palpable proof of a failure, and in “Where the River Ran,” it closes the curtain on a kind of dream-like state. (Whether that’s good or bad depends on how you perceive this dream.)

So in the end, there was no deliberately arranged sequence of functions for the motif of the sun, just its role as judge and executioner in a given situation. I couldn’t even say if there is a linear narrative on the album or a red thread… maybe just a silver lining…

Karo: Your lyrics repeatedly return to a very physical vocabulary: milk, poison, ashes, stone, water, fire, wounds, walls, gates, mirrors. Abstract emotions are almost always given material form. Is that something you consciously look for when writing, the moment when an emotion can be translated into an object, substance or landscape?

Peer: That’s a very interesting question. To answer it, let me briefly describe my way of writing.

When it comes to words, I’m not a messenger but see myself more as an observer. That means I don’t have to find proper ways of wrapping a certain message or statement in adequate syllables. I just describe what is reflected on inner surfaces, light mirrored and light absorbed… camera obscura in my head.

Maybe I need those objects because of their reflective qualities, because of their physical necessity. Who equips our dreams? Who tells our subconscious which archetypes are valid and which are not? Is the stone really a stone or just a tool to break the mirror?

I don’t look for objects. I try to remember them…

Karo: “Resistance” contains a particularly interesting sequence: “I am the enemy,” “I am the strategy,” “I am the remedy,” “I am the empathy.” The speaker seems to occupy conflicting positions within the same struggle. Is resistance on this album directed against something outside the self, or are you more interested in the ways we become simultaneously the source of our own damage and the means of surviving it?

Peer: I was thinking a lot about these words. While writing them and afterwards.

Which of these four conditions am I really? And how many of them can you be at the same time? And why not all?

I think it’s not anger about a state but a revolt against its limitations. Not resistance against an external system, but resistance against a final form. Against definition. Against the temptation to trade complexity for peace.

Half-damaged instead of neatly resolved.

Karo: In “City Walls,” the questions gradually move from “Where is my ambition?” and “Where is my desire?” toward “Where am I?” and finally “Who am I?” I find that progression fascinating because architecture begins to feel psychological. Do cities interest you as emotional structures, places we construct around ourselves but also internalise?

Peer: Isn’t it true that language constructs its own spaces? Walls of repetitions, gates through semantic shifts, interiors built from omission… where the self is not negotiated psychologically but cartographically. It’s not what I am, but where. Dislocated between inner condition and external geography.

Is a wall protecting or imprisoning? Does a gate promise shelter or a chance to escape? Or is it just a symbol of transition? What if all the cities, walls and gates are not places of salvation but engineered systems of survival?

Let’s not be misled by the colour white. It doesn’t have to mean purity. Maybe it’s just sterility.

Where am I?

It’s all the way we left…

Karo: “Dreams (Gone By)” turns dreams into dew, poison, milk and ashes, while the rest of the lyric repeatedly creates, worships, destroys and loses them. Do you see memory in a similar way, not as something fixed that we retrieve, but as something that changes its substance every time we return to it?

Peer: It’s their texture that makes memories so unpredictable. Their nature. Not only when it comes to our decision about what eventually finds its way into the storage room of our heads, but also what form it will take.

Memories can be so sheltering, so soothing and consoling. They can catch you and drop you gently onto a soft surface, warm waters… floating… or they can be seething and boiling, burn your flesh and cauterize your skin and thoughts.

Sometimes at the same time… without changing their dress.

“My memories – my silence… and I don’t mind the flames…”

Karo: Musically, one of the things I find distinctive about Golden Apes is the coexistence of considerable physical weight with something almost fragile. The guitars can be massive and the drums forceful, yet the songs still retain air, distance and dreamlike movement. When arranging a song, how conscious are you of that balance between density and space? Is knowing what to remove now as important as knowing what to add?

Peer: I think this is even one of the most important things when it comes to creating a song – to let things breathe, to value the sound by granting it silence.

It’s something we did wrong so often, trying to emphasise a certain feeling or atmosphere by covering it with layers of sonic attributes until it disappeared under all this weight.

I’ve always felt a song to be a bit like light entering a room. You have the illuminated areas, the bright and sometimes overexposed spots, and you have the places where no light can crawl. And you have the places in between, the blurred and indistinct ones… the undecided.

And all together, they make you understand the room, let you guess its architecture. You will never really know what’s in the dark corners, but it’s part of the picture.

Karo: Peer, your voice has such a deep and immediately identifiable resonance that it could very easily dominate these songs, yet on this album it often feels embedded inside the arrangements rather than placed above them. Has your relationship with your own voice changed over the years, particularly in terms of restraint, vulnerability and how much emotion you choose to expose directly?

Peer: First of all, thank you for these flattering and charming words. You should know that I’ve never been unshakeably convinced of my vocal abilities. But yes, after learning about the possibilities and realising the limitations, I feel more confident with my voice.

It’s always some kind of balancing act between seeing the voice simply as an instrument that adds another colour to the canvas and experiencing your own voice as something that communicates all the black and white, the highs and lows that are in your head, which can be very intimate and revealing.

But on the one hand, this is part of the “game.” On the other hand, I guess I’ve found a way to be quite generous with the possibilities of reading and interpreting the lyrics – not for safety reasons, but because I like layering meanings and ciphers and leaving enough space between the lines.

I don’t choose or weigh the amount of emotion my voice might convey through the words. It’s simply the way I feel them…

Karo: I saw Golden Apes at Dark Spring this year, and what struck me again is how differently these songs behave once they become physical performances. Dark Spring is also a festival you curate yourselves. Does spending an entire day surrounded by artists you have deliberately chosen change the way you experience your own performance that evening? Is there a dialogue between the programme you construct and the version of Golden Apes that eventually walks onto the stage?

This year’s edition at Berlin’s Lido brought Golden Apes together with Corpus Delicti, Klez.e, The Devil & The Universe and Varg I Veum.

Peer: I couldn’t even tell you that there are different versions of the band onstage!

As you probably know, when we take the stage, there’s no prepared concept, no elaborate plan or staged execution. It is – as simple as it sounds – four guys playing some songs. And all the parameters that influence the density, intensity and energy are at work, live, in that very moment.

It’s the people, of course, it’s the room, it’s the sound, it’s the texture of the songs themselves or the colour in your head on that day… many things can influence what is happening there on stage.

Of course, it’s inspiring and energising to see other bands perform, to feel the sound, the atmosphere they create and the music acting as a catalyst for your own emotional state, but always in some kind of triggering way, never by comparing or judging.

Karo: I will see you again in Wrocław very soon, this time in a rather different context: the 30th anniversary of Liverpool club and the Castle Party Halloween night. You have played festivals, large stages and clubs across many countries. Does a small club carrying decades of its own scene history demand a different kind of performance from you than a festival stage does, especially with an album as inward and atmospheric as this one?

Golden Apes were scheduled for the October 31 anniversary night in Wrocław alongside Her Own World and Shadows Veil.

Peer: Of course, it’s different whether you’re standing on a big stage at a festival, maybe even in daylight, or on a small one in a foggy room. And for sure, both versions have their own special and unique influence on the way we feel and the way the music feels while performing.

But as I said – it’s nothing that’s planned. It’s this combination of external circumstances and inner condition. And I like both situations very much because they cast a different light on the way you feel the songs in that moment.

There’s something special about seeing the sky above you while singing, just as it’s intense to have the audience an arm’s length away during the show. I can’t even tell you which feels more appropriate for the songs.

It’s a bit like looking at a painting at different times of the day, in different light. It’s the same painting, but its effect can be completely different.

By the way – now that the evening in Wrocław has already taken place, I can tell you how brilliant it was and how much joy it was to play this show. The Liverpool club is really a special venue, and the atmosphere was amazing…

Karo: The album contains several forms of continuation, but very little uncomplicated triumph: the new day in “Resistance” is “not yet bright,” the sun rises in “Helion,” “Evelyn” promises a return that remains somewhere in the future, and the final song looks back at dreams that have already gone.

Do you think “The Sun Came Up Tremendously” ultimately deals less with overcoming darkness than with learning how different states of loss, hope, fear and renewal can exist simultaneously?

Peer: I never really thought about the album in its entirety in this strictly conceptual and narrative way, but if I did, I’d say it is about the balance and the proportion of light and shadow in all things. It is about their dependence on each other and their existential necessity to make the opposing state possible in the first place.

Sure, there can be no shadow without light, but also, what is the point of hope if there’s no presence of hopelessness? And of course, the sun rises only and solely from the dark.

There is not a single state without the other, and we all know that this is what life is about. About the spark even in the blackest darkness and the awareness of the approaching night on a warm, yellow summer day.

It is all there. Laws of physics, laws of emotions…

About Golden Apes

Golden Apes are a German post-punk, darkwave and gothic rock band formed in Berlin in 1998. Centred around vocalist, lyricist and composer Peer Lebrecht, the group has developed a distinctive sound combining atmospheric guitar arrangements, prominent basslines, melodic intensity and poetic, frequently surreal lyrics.

Their debut album, “Stigma 3,” appeared in 2000, followed by a succession of releases including “Thalassemia,” “The Geometry of Tempest,” “The Langsyne Litanies,” “MALVS,” “KASBEK” and “Our Ashes at the End of the Day”. Throughout their career, Golden Apes have toured internationally and appeared at events including Wave-Gotik-Treffen and Castle Party.

Their twelfth studio album, “The Sun Came Up Tremendously,” was released on September 18, 2026, through Icy Cold Records. Recorded and mixed at Thommy Hein Studios in Berlin, the album features Peer Lebrecht (vocals, synthesizers), Maximilian Hennig (guitar), Stephan Schönfeld (guitar), Christian Lebrecht (bass) and Salomon Bosse (drums), with additional guitar contributions from Thommy Hein. Side-Line reviewed the album in October 2026, and the band closed out October with a 30th-anniversary show at Wrocław’s Liverpool club during Castle Party’s Halloween night. Golden Apes’ official site is at goldenapes.com, with the catalogue available via Bandcamp.

items.title: Sandie Trash shares ‘On n’est jamais que des filles’ featuring Emmanuelle 5
items.summary: French artist Sandie Trash releases "On n'est jamais que des filles," featuring Emmanuelle 5, the second single from "Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka."
items.fullText:
French artist Sandie Trash has released “On n’est jamais que des filles,” featuring Emmanuelle 5, the second single from her upcoming album “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka.” Sandie Trash describes the project as working within French chanson, while her own promotional material places it within post-punk.

“On n’est jamais que des filles” is available on Sandie Trash’s Bandcamp page.

Credits for ‘On n’est jamais que des filles’

Emmanuelle 5, also known for her work with Dead Sexy, provides vocals on the track. The song is mixed by Eric Débris, of the French punk band Métal Urbain, and mastered at ATX Mastering Studio. “On n’est jamais que des filles” follows “Poupée Panik,” featuring Eric Débris and Richard Belgium, as the second extract from the forthcoming nine-track album “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka.”

About Sandie Trash

Sandie Trash is a French artist based in Périgueux. Her music moves between chanson and post-punk-influenced songwriting, built around narrative themes she has described as shifting between sex and violence within a noir fiction setting.

Side-Line covered the first single from “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka,” “Poupée Panik,” in September 2026. “On n’est jamais que des filles” continues the same album campaign, again featuring a guest contribution from Eric Débris of Métal Urbain.

items.title: Ductape release new video for ‘D.E.R.T’ off ‘Faded Flowers’
items.summary: Post-punk duo Ductape release a new video for "D.E.R.T," the sixth video from their album "Faded Flowers," directed by Begüm Koçum.
items.fullText:
Post-punk and darkwave duo Ductape have released a new video for “D.E.R.T,” a track from their album “Faded Flowers”. It is the sixth video the duo have issued from the album, which came out September 18, 2026, on vinyl and CD.

Credits for the ‘D.E.R.T’ video

The video was photographed and directed by Begüm Koçum, with artist styling by Bedirhan Tasci and costume design by Ziya Kocaturk. Efe Demirtas handled lighting and backstage video assistance, with Rumeysa Arslan as second assistant, Burcin Papuccular on moon design, and production by Azize Istanbul Design Studio.

About Ductape

Ductape is a post-punk and darkwave duo of Çağla Güleray, on vocals and synthesizer, and Furkan Güleray, on guitar, bass and drum programming. The project began in Istanbul before the pair relocated their creative base to France.

Side-Line covered the announcement of Ductape’s fourth album, “Faded Flowers,” in August 2026, ahead of its September 18 release on vinyl and CD. The video for “D.E.R.T” is the sixth the duo have released from that album, continuing a video campaign built with the same creative team behind their other “Faded Flowers” clips.

items.title: Peter Christopherson’s ‘Time Machines II’ arrives on vinyl and CD
items.summary: Peter Christopherson's "Time Machines II," first issued as a limited 2014 memory stick, is now available on vinyl and CD through Infinite Fog.
items.fullText:
“Time Machines II,” a set of unfinished works by the late Peter Christopherson of Coil, is now available on vinyl and CD for the first time through Infinite Fog. The seven tracks had previously circulated only as a limited deluxe memory stick edition compiled in 2014, four years after Christopherson’s death, which sold out almost immediately.

Credits and format for ‘Time Machines II’

The seven tracks, titled “Untitled I” through “Untitled VII,” were assembled by people close to Christopherson after his death in 2010. The title references Coil’s 1998 album “Time Machines,” though Infinite Fog’s release notes describe “Time Machines II” as musically distinct from that record. The album is mastered by Jessica Thompson, who has worked on previous Coil reissues for the label, and is available on black vinyl, on a limited clear vinyl edition, and on CD in a digipak.

About Peter Christopherson

Peter Christopherson, known to collaborators as Sleazy, was a founding member of Coil alongside John Balance, and had earlier been part of Throbbing Gristle. Following Balance’s death in 2004, Christopherson continued recording new material until his own death in 2010, leaving several projects at different stages of completion.

In 2014, people close to Christopherson compiled seven of these unfinished pieces as “Time Machines II,” issued in a limited deluxe memory stick edition that sold out quickly and became a sought-after collector’s item. Infinite Fog’s vinyl and CD release makes the material available in physical formats for the first time.

items.title: Kommando compiles 1994 recordings on ‘Electronic Spasm’ CD
items.summary: Kommando, the project of Dan Courtman, compiles its 1994 cassette recordings on the CD "Electronic Spasm," out November 11, 2026, via Ant-Zen.
items.fullText:
Kommando, a project conceived by Dan Courtman as the darker counterpart to his Thorofon alter ego, will release “Electronic Spasm” on November 11, 2026, through Ant-Zen. The eleven-track CD compiles the project’s earliest recordings, made in 1993 and 1994 and self-released at the time as two cassette albums.

Tracklist and credits for ‘Electronic Spasm’

The two source cassettes, “Electronic Fear” and “Funky Spasm,” were originally released in 1994. “Electronic Spasm” gathers the surviving recordings from both onto one eleven-track CD: “Spasm 1,” “Spasm 2,” “Mental Funkyard 1” through “Mental Funkyard 4,” “Fear 1” through “Fear 3,” and “Clinical Death 1” and “Clinical Death 2.” The material was recorded and produced by Kommando in 1993 and 1994, remastered in 2026, with layout by Salt. “Electronic Spasm” is available as a digital album and on CD in a matte six-panel digipak.

About Kommando

Kommando is a project of musician Dan Courtman, conceived as a darker, more anxiety-inducing counterpart to his better-known alter ego Thorofon. Its earliest recordings date to 1993, self-released the following year as the cassette albums “Electronic Fear” and “Funky Spasm.”

“Electronic Spasm,” out November 11, 2026, on Ant-Zen, compiles the surviving material from both cassettes, documenting the formative recordings behind a project that would continue under the Kommando name alongside Courtman’s work as Thorofon.

items.title: Michael Idehall sets ‘Vessel’ album for November 18 on Ant-Zen
items.summary: Swedish artist Michael Idehall releases the album "Vessel" on November 18, 2026, via Ant-Zen and Beläten, on digital and 12" vinyl.
items.fullText:
Swedish multidisciplinary artist Michael Idehall will release the album “Vessel” on November 18, 2026, through Ant-Zen and Beläten. The ten-track record draws on sacred and apocalyptic literature as a framework for the post-industrial and dark ambient soundscapes Idehall builds across his work as a musician, writer and painter.

Tracklist and credits for ‘Vessel’

“Vessel” runs ten tracks, opening with “This Is Bardo” and closing with “Resin on the Mirror (Oneiric Dirge),” drawing track titles from sources including the I Ching and the Mahabharata. The album is mastered by Nÿland, with visual realization by Nullvoid and packaging concept by Salt. It is available as a digital album and on 12″ vinyl, pressed on grey marbled vinyl in a matte black die-cut sleeve.

About Michael Idehall

Michael Idehall is a Swedish multidisciplinary artist, musician, writer and painter whose work combines post-industrial music, dark ambient soundscapes and ritualistic elements. Idehall has released several titles through Ant-Zen, including the EP “Serving With Both Hands” in March 2022 and the album “Apokryphos” in November 2024.

“Vessel,” out November 18, 2026, on Ant-Zen and Beläten, continues that catalogue, using sacred literature as a lens for the cyclical themes of consciousness and violence that run through the album’s ten tracks.

items.title: Control sets ‘Enemy’ album for November 13 on Ant-Zen
items.summary: Control, the power electronics project of Thomas Garrison, releases the album "Enemy" on November 13, 2026, via Ant-Zen and Raubbau.
items.fullText:
Control, the power electronics and death industrial project of American musician Thomas Garrison, will release the album “Enemy” on November 13, 2026, through Ant-Zen and Raubbau. The six-track record follows Garrison’s work since the late 1990s treating distortion, saturation and volume as deliberate compositional tools.

Tracklist and format for Control’s ‘Enemy’

“Enemy” moves across six tracks from an unsettled opening mood through escalating aggression to a bleaker close: “Imperative,” “Enemy,” “Failed State,” “Tyranny,” “Shutdown” and “War of the Innocence.” The album is mastered by Paul Lavigne at Kontrast Mastering, with layout by Stefan Alt. It is available as a digital album and on 12″ vinyl, each copy pressed in a unique multicoloured blend and including a digital download code.

About Control

Control is the solo power electronics and death industrial project of American musician Thomas Garrison, active since the late 1990s. Garrison’s work under the Control name treats distortion, saturation and volume as deliberate compositional tools, built to create tension and psychological unease across long-form pieces.

“Enemy,” released November 13, 2026, on Ant-Zen and Raubbau, is Garrison’s latest album under the Control name, continuing a catalogue built within the power electronics and death industrial underground.

items.title: Split Vision – Higher Love
items.summary: Not a Depeche Mode cover version, but sophisticated synth pop track. Discover how Split Vision breathe new life into the spirit of the 80s on “Higher Love”.
items.fullText:
Far from what you’d expect from a cover version: Split Vision impress with “Higher Love”

I must dis­ap­point every Depeche Mode fan right from the start. This is because “Higher Love” is not a cov­er ver­sion of the track of the same name from “Songs Of Faith And Devotion”. However, that does not in any way make this new single from Sweden any less impressive.

After all, the duo are known for their con­sist­ent synth pop sound, which is also evid­ent on this track from their latest album, “BetaCity”. The tried-and-tested blend of clas­sic 80s syn­thes­isers, driv­ing beats, emotive vocals and instantly catchy melod­ies meshes seam­lessly here. Without being a mere copy, this cre­ates an authen­t­ic sound that pays homage to its music­al roots whilst retain­ing a dis­tinct iden­tity of its own.
