items.title: Jean-Michel Jarre releases ‘Machines: A History of Electronic Music’
items.summary: Jean-Michel Jarre publishes "Machines: A History of Electronic Music" via Thames & Hudson, out November 5, 2026, with Gary Numan, Vince Clarke and more.
items.fullText:
French electronic music pioneer Jean-Michel Jarre has published ‘Machines: A History of Electronic Music’, a 368-page illustrated hardcover released through Thames & Hudson on November 5, 2026. The book traces more than a century of electronic sound through instruments drawn from Jarre’s own collection, with around 800 illustrations and reflections from fellow musicians.

The book opens with Luigi Russolo’s 1913 Futurist manifesto “The Art of Noises” and moves through early radio experiments, tape manipulation, analogue synthesizers, digital technology and recent developments involving artificial intelligence. Around 150 machines from Jarre’s archive of electronic and electroacoustic instruments, among the largest private collections of its kind, illustrate the chapters, combined with rare photographs, historical material and personal anecdotes. Jarre also recounts his own path into the field, from a childhood fascination with tape recorders to his studies under Pierre Schaeffer in Paris.

Contributors to the book include Armin van Buuren, Vince Clarke (Erasure, Yazoo, Depeche Mode), Gillian Gilbert (New Order), Nicolas Godin (Air), Richie Hawtin, Johnny Marr (The Smiths), Gary Numan, Benjamin John Power (Blanck Mass, Fuck Buttons), Nick Rhodes (Duran Duran), Pete Townshend (The Who) and Hans Zimmer. Side-Line previously covered two of Jarre’s collaborations with contributors to the book: a reworked “Automatic” with Vince Clarke in 2015, and the Gary Numan-featuring follow-up to “Electronica 1: The Time Machine” in 2016.

‘Machines: A History of Electronic Music’ is available in the UK, Australia and through booksellers across Europe. Further editions are planned for France, Poland and North America.

About Jean-Michel Jarre

Jean-Michel Jarre is a French composer and producer whose career in electronic music spans more than five decades. He studied under Pierre Schaeffer at the Groupe de Recherches Musicales in Paris, grounding his later work in the musique concrète tradition before moving into synthesizer-based composition. His 1976 album “Oxygène” established him internationally and set the template for the large-scale outdoor concerts he later staged around the world.

Jarre has continued to record and perform through the following decades, including the “Electronica” project, released across two volumes beginning in 2015 and built around collaborations with artists including Gary Numan, Vince Clarke, Pet Shop Boys and Tangerine Dream’s Edgar Froese. Alongside his recording career, Jarre has assembled a private collection of electronic and electroacoustic instruments spanning the history of the medium, from early experimental devices to modular synthesizers and one-off prototypes.

‘Machines: A History of Electronic Music’ draws directly on that archive. Published by Thames & Hudson on November 5, 2026, the book combines instruments from Jarre’s collection with contributions from musicians including Gary Numan, Vince Clarke, Gillian Gilbert, Nick Rhodes and Johnny Marr, placing his own history within a broader account of electronic music’s technological development.

items.title: I-M-R announces digital compilation ‘Shreds of Time 2012-20’
items.summary: German darkwave project I-M-R, the continuation of In My Rosary, compiles tracks from four albums on "Shreds of Time 2012-20," via Bandcamp.
items.fullText:
German darkwave and darkfolk project I-M-R has released the digital compilation “Shreds of Time 2012-20” through Bandcamp, gathering 12 tracks drawn from its four albums released since 2012: “Letters from the Paper Garden,” “InOutSide,” “25.20.15” and “Follow the Ruins.” Ralf Jesek, who leads the project, announced the release for November 30, 2026, in a press email; the Bandcamp page itself lists a release date of November 6, 2026.

The tracklist draws one or more songs from each of the four source albums, several featuring guest vocalists: “By the Fire” with Annette Kosakowski, “Poisoned Eyes” with Derrière Le Miroir, “The Paper Garden” with Isabelle Dekeyser, “Words” with Elena Fossi, “She Said” with Kriistal Ann and “Masquerade” with Stillife, alongside “Never…Again,” “The Golden Haze,” “Night,” “Nothing Left,” “Something in Dead Eyes” and “We Cannot Change.” All four source albums were released by Syborgmusic.

“Shreds of Time 2012-20” is available as a digital album on Bandcamp.

About I-M-R

I-M-R, based in Karlsruhe, Germany, is the continuation of In My Rosary, a darkwave and darkfolk project founded in 1992 by composer, singer and producer Ralf Jesek together with lyricist and photographer Dirk Lakomy. Under that name, the pair released around a dozen albums internationally. After Lakomy left the project in 2011, Jesek continued it as I-M-R, working with live guest musicians Martin von Arndt, also known for his work with Printed at Bismarck’s Death, and Holger Diener.

Since 2012, I-M-R has released four albums through Syborgmusic: “Letters from the Paper Garden,” “InOutSide,” “25.20.15” and “Follow the Ruins.” The project’s most recent release is the eight-track “Follow the Ruins EP,” also issued by Syborgmusic. “Shreds of Time 2012-20” draws together tracks from across that catalogue into a single compilation.

items.title: Pop Will Eat Itself announce ‘Life Begins @ PWEI.40’ for February 2027
items.summary: Pop Will Eat Itself mark 40 years with the album "Life Begins @ PWEI.40," out February 19, 2027, and four UK live dates starting November 13.
items.fullText:
Pop Will Eat Itself founders Graham Crabb and Adam Mole will release the album “Life Begins @ PWEI.40” on February 19, 2027, marking 40 years of the band. The record reworks tracks from across the band’s catalogue with a cast of guest collaborators, and is accompanied by four UK live dates beginning November 13.

The album draws on PWEI songs including “1000 X No,” “Get the Girl,” “Kill the Baddies,” “There Is a Psychopath in My Soup,” “Mother,” “Dance of the Mad,” “I’m Sniffin’ with You Hoo,” “88 Seconds & Still Counting” and “Bulletproof,” reworked with contributions from Stephen Mallinder of Cabaret Voltaire, Brian Tatler of Diamond Head and Saxon, Karl Willetts of Bolt Thrower and Memoriam, Mark Gemini Thwaite of The Wonder Stuff and Peter Murphy’s band, Clams Baker of Warmduscher, Fluke, Meryl Streek and Rachel Mayfield. Ken Scott and Rocco Barker of Wasted Youth appear on a reworking of their song “I Wish I Was a Girl.” Two newly written PWEI tracks are also included: “I Don’t Wanna Dance,” featuring Vita of THR0B, and “Night Shift Riot,” featuring guitar from Mark Gemini Thwaite.

A separate 7-inch single reworks “Ich Bin Ein Ausländer,” with interpretations by original PWEI member Clint Mansell and Los Angeles outfit clipping., featuring Sara Taylor of Youth Code and Sharon Udoh. A bonus vinyl collection, “Lost Treasures & Unearthed Gems,” gathers 12 previously unreleased PWEI recordings with sleeve notes by Adam Mole and Paul Snell. The album’s sleeve design comes from Ian Anderson and The Designers Republic, who also designed PWEI’s original 1990s artwork.

‘Life Begins @ PWEI.40’ formats

  • Limited edition gatefold double vinyl: the album on hot pink vinyl, with the “Lost Treasures & Unearthed Gems” bonus album on canary yellow vinyl and a PWEI.40 bin sticker
  • Limited edition deluxe vinyl: the album on neon magenta vinyl, with the “Ich Bin Ein Ausländer” 7-inch as a bonus disc
  • Deluxe CD: the album in a book pack, with two additional previously unreleased recordings not featured on the vinyl bonus release

‘Life Begins @ PWEI.40’ tracklist

Side one – “Sticky,” featuring Karl Willetts – “Night Shift Riot,” featuring Mark Gemini Thwaite – “1000 X No,” featuring Stephen Mallinder – “Just Gotta Say It” – “Mother,” featuring Rachel Mayfield – “Car Chase,” featuring Brian Tatler – “Car Crash,” featuring Brian Tatler – “Dance of the Mad Bastards,” reworked by Fluke

Side two – “Psychopath in My Soup,” featuring Karl Willetts – “Ruff Justice,” featuring Clams Baker – “Don’t Wanna Dance,” featuring Vita – “Poppies Go Boom!,” featuring Mark Gemini Thwaite – “I Wish I Was A Girl,” featuring Ken Scott and Rocco Barker – “Bite the Bullet,” reworked by Meryl Streek

Tour dates for Pop Will Eat Itself

Crabb and Mole take the PWEI.40 project on the road for four UK dates in late 2026:

  • November 13: Shiiine On Festival, Minehead
  • November 26: 93 Feet East, London, with guest So Good
  • November 27: Network, Sheffield, with guest So Good
  • December 5: Stourbridge Town Hall, Stourbridge, with Jonn and Rat performing as Neds Acoustic Dustbin, plus a screening of the previously unreleased 1994 tour film “Amalgamation,” filmed at two sold-out Aston Villa Leisure Centre shows

About Pop Will Eat Itself

Pop Will Eat Itself formed in Stourbridge, England, in 1986, initially known as a grebo act before the band’s sound shifted toward sample-driven indie and industrial rock. Graham Crabb, originally the band’s drummer, moved to vocals and fronted the group until leaving in 1995; Adam Mole has played guitars, keyboards and programming since the band’s formation. Clint Mansell was part of the band’s original lineup before leaving the project; he went on to score films including “Requiem for a Dream,” “The Fountain,” “Moon” and “Black Swan.”

Crabb left Pop Will Eat Itself in 1995 and later ran the ambient side project Golden Claw Musics; he returned as the band’s sole original member in a 2011 lineup, and Mole rejoined in 2018. For the 40th-anniversary project PWEI.40, Crabb and Mole reworked tracks from across the band’s catalogue with an “unlikely cast of collaborators,” among them Cabaret Voltaire’s Stephen Mallinder, Bolt Thrower’s Karl Willetts and original member Clint Mansell. The result is the album “Life Begins @ PWEI.40,” set for release on February 19, 2027, alongside a bonus vinyl collection of unreleased archive recordings and a reworked 7-inch single. PWEI.40 plays four UK dates starting November 13, 2026, ahead of the album’s release.

items.title: Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? announces digital reissues and new album for 2027
items.summary: German EBM act Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? reissues its 1990s catalogue via Sub Culture Records from November 13, with a vinyl EP and new album due in 2027.
items.fullText:
German EBM and electro-punk act Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? is reissuing its 1990s catalogue digitally through Norwegian label Sub Culture Records. A new vinyl EP and a full studio album follow in 2027. The campaign begins November 13 with the digital reissue of “Annorlunda” (1994) and the album “Les Enfants Sauvages” (1995).

Sub Culture Records, run by longtime friend of the band Per Aksel Lundgreen, is bringing Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.?’s earlier recordings to streaming and download platforms for the first time. Further digital reissues are expected in the coming months, including material from the 1993 album “Tumulte” and other recordings from the band’s 1990s catalogue.

Alongside the reissues, Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? are preparing new material through Germany’s Emmo.biz Records. A limited-edition 12-inch vinyl EP, “No Bottom – No Top”, is scheduled for January 15, 2027. It carries two new compositions, “The Flood” and “Impuls Kontakt”, alongside reworked versions of “Souvenir” and “Ewigkeit”. A full-length studio album is also planned for later in 2027; the band describe the new material as retaining their combination of EBM, industrial electronics and electro-punk, with driving bass sequences, hard rhythms and a more contemporary production approach. No album title or exact release date has been set.

About Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.?

Sabotage Q.C.Q.C.? is a German EBM and electro-punk act whose recorded history stretches back more than three decades, including the albums “Tumulte” (1993), “Annorlunda” (1994) and “Les Enfants Sauvages” (1995). With the 1990s catalogue now heading to digital platforms through Sub Culture Records and new material in preparation through Emmo.biz Records, the band have a full release schedule planned through 2027: the digital reissues from November 2026, the “No Bottom – No Top” vinyl EP in January 2027, and a new studio album later in the year.

items.title: Local Blood releases self-titled third album ‘Local Blood’
items.summary: Vilnius post-punk band Local Blood release their self-titled third album on Bandcamp and streaming platforms, and start a European tour November 13.
items.fullText:
Vilnius, Lithuania alternative rock and post-punk band Local Blood released their third studio album, the self-titled “Local Blood”, on November 5 across streaming platforms, with a 12-inch vinyl edition available for pre-order. The four-piece begin a European tour in the same week.

The self-titled record follows “Dystopian Disco” (2022) and “Loverman” (2023), and was recorded during the summer of 2026. It blends the band’s post-punk energy with dark melodies, alternative rock influences and an intense emotional atmosphere. The self-titled choice marks what the band describe as a return to their own identity while continuing to explore new sounds and directions. The lead single, “ŠUOKIS”, is the band’s first recording in the Samogitian dialect of Lithuanian.

Local Blood begin a European tour on November 13, playing Poland, Hungary, France and Germany in support of the new album.

“Local Blood” is available on Bandcamp and Spotify, with the 12-inch vinyl edition available to pre-order through the band.

About Local Blood

Local Blood is a four-piece alternative rock and post-punk band from Vilnius, Lithuania. The band released their debut album “Dystopian Disco” in 2022, followed by “Loverman” in 2023, before returning in 2026 with their self-titled third album. Known for blending post-punk energy with dark melodies and alternative rock influences, Local Blood have previously toured Europe and continue to build an international following with “ŠUOKIS”, their first song recorded in the Samogitian dialect of Lithuanian, and the self-titled album it introduces.

Then Comes Silence have toured extensively across Europe, North America and Latin America, sharing stages with Fields of the Nephilim, Clan of Xymox, The Chameleons, A Place to Bury Strangers, Pink Turns Blue and The Bellwether Syndicate, and playing festivals including M’era Luna, Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Amphi Festival, Castle Party, Tomorrow’s Ghosts Festival and W-Festival. items.title: Killing Joke’s ‘Brighter Than a Thousand Suns’ turns 40 on 10 November
items.summary: Killing Joke released "Brighter Than a Thousand Suns" on 10 November 1986 through E.G. Records. The album turns 40 this year.
items.fullText:
English post-punk band Killing Joke released their sixth studio album, “Brighter Than a Thousand Suns,” on 10 November 1986 through E.G. Records, the band’s first album to reach shops through a Virgin Records deal. The album turns 40 this year.

Most of “Brighter Than a Thousand Suns” was recorded in Berlin in October 1985 with Chris Kimsey, who had also produced the preceding album, “Night Time.” Two further tracks followed in 1986: “Victory” and “Ecstasy,” produced by Stewart Levine in March, and “A Southern Sky,” produced by Chris Tsangarides in August. E.G. Records had Kimsey’s mixes replaced with new mixes by Julian Mendelsohn aimed at wider commercial appeal, against the band’s own preference; those Mendelsohn mixes went out on the original release, with “Victory” extended past seven minutes. Killing Joke headlined the first day of the 1986 Reading Festival on 22 August and played most of the album live there before release. A 2008 CD remaster restored Kimsey’s original mixes at the band’s request and added bonus tracks.

The album featured Jaz Coleman on vocals and keyboards, Kevin “Geordie” Walker on guitar, Paul Raven on bass and Paul Ferguson on drums and vocals. “Adorations” came out as a single in August 1986, followed by “Sanity” in October. “Brighter Than a Thousand Suns” entered the UK Albums Chart at number 54, where it stayed for one week, and reached number 194 on the US Billboard 200. The original vinyl pressing held eight tracks; the cassette and CD carried the full eleven:

  1. “Adorations”
  2. “Sanity”
  3. “Chessboards”
  4. “Twilight of the Mortal”
  5. “Love of the Masses”
  6. “A Southern Sky”
  7. “Victory”
  8. “Wintergardens”
  9. “Rubicon”
  10. “Goodbye to the Village”
  11. “Exile”

“Brighter Than a Thousand Suns” is available as a digital album on Spotify.

About Killing Joke

Killing Joke formed in October 1978 in Notting Hill, London. Jaz Coleman (vocals, keyboards) and Paul Ferguson (drums) placed a Melody Maker ad in February 1979 that brought in guitarist Kevin “Geordie” Walker and bassist Martin “Youth” Glover, completing the original line-up. The band self-released its early material on its own Malicious Damage label, including the “Turn to Red” EP in October 1979, the “Almost Red” EP that November and the “Nervous System” single in December 1979.

The self-titled debut album followed on 5 October 1980 through E.G. Records, recorded at Marquee Studios that August, its 46th anniversary covered by Side-Line. Killing Joke continued with “What’s THIS For…!” in 1981 and “Revelations” in 1982, after which Youth left the band and Paul Raven took over on bass. “Fire Dances” followed in 1983 and “Night Time” in 1985, both before Chris Kimsey returned to produce “Brighter Than a Thousand Suns” in 1986, the first Killing Joke album to reach shops through a Virgin Records deal.

Killing Joke’s catalogue continued through “Outside the Gate” (1988), “Extremities, Dirt and Various Repressed Emotions” (1990), “Pandemonium” (1994), “Democracy” (1996), a second self-titled album (2003), “Hosannas From the Basements of Hell” (2006), “Absolute Dissent” (2010), “MMXII” (2012) and “Pylon” (2015). Coleman and Walker remained the band’s only constant members until Walker’s death in November 2023 at age 64. “Brighter Than a Thousand Suns,” the album that brought the band its first release through a Virgin Records deal and its Berlin studio sessions with Chris Kimsey, turns 40 this November.

items.title: This Morn’Omina – Vestiges (Digital/CD Album – ProNoize / Dark Dimensions)
items.summary: The Belgian project This Morn’Omina celebrates its thirtieth anniversary this year. Founded and consistently driven...
items.fullText:
The Belgian project This Morn’Omina celebrates its thirtieth anniversary this year. Founded and consistently driven by Mika Goedrijk, the project has left an indelible impression on anyone who has ever experienced This Morn’Omina performing live. This is largely due to the distinctive style the project embodies—a blend of Industrial, Electro, Trance, and Tribal influences. Added to this are deeply spiritual and mystical themes, which have frequently resulted in the release of trilogies. These works often form complete cycles, a pattern briefly interrupted by this compilation, which features several previously unreleased versions. Mika Goedrijk deliberately avoids calling it a ‘best of’, preferring the term ‘part of’.

Musically, This Morn’Omina remains a unique experience, with no real equivalent. Various influences are woven together into an overwhelming production that can appeal to a broader audience. Moreover, the compositions and production are meticulously crafted, with every element developed down to the finest detail. The rhythms quickly induce a state of ecstasy, creating a genuine Trance-like experience through their repetitive, crescendo-driven structures, complemented by rich, atmospheric textures that often carry an Eastern flavour. This is particularly evident on the only live track included in the collection. Although This Morn’Omina will always be associated with its major hit, “One Eyed Man”—featured here in an alternative version—there are plenty of other tracks well worth exploring. In recent years, Mika Goedrijk has also started incorporating vocals, although the voice primarily serves as a complementary element, enhancing the music and reinforcing its underlying themes. This compilation is clearly just a ‘part of’ something much larger, as many other tracks could easily have found their place here.

This Morn’Omina remains a grandmaster of a genre it has almost single-handedly developed—a genre that has continued to evolve over the years, as evidenced by Mika Goedrijk’s latest album, “Insha,” released earlier this year on Cyclic Law. (Rating:9).

Listen to “One Eyed-Man (Liber III)”:

About This Morn’Omina

Formed in 1996 in Belgium, This Morn’Omina is the ritual industrial project of Mika Goedrijk. Its sound moves through ceremonial percussion, hypnotic repetition, martial pressure, EBM structures and Middle Eastern tonal references, using rhythm as a form of invocation rather than a straightforward club mechanism.

Across releases including “7 Years Of Famine,” “Le Serpent Blanc – Le Serpent Rouge” and “Les Passages Jumeaux,” This Morn’Omina built a catalogue organized around cycles such as Hegira, Nyan and the ongoing Kundalini trilogy. “One-Eyed Man” became an early club-level reference point for the project, though its work has always extended beyond dancefloor function. In January 2026, Mika Goedrijk released “Insha,” the opening chapter of the Kundalini trilogy, on Cyclic Law and Zazen Sounds.

In June 2026, Side-Line reported that This Morn’Omina had joined the Dark Dimensions Label Group, with ProNoize / Dark Dimensions set to issue “Vestiges – 30 Years Of Ritual Sound (1996-2026)” as a limited digipak CD on 26 June 2026. Mika Goedrijk discussed the compilation’s selection process, built around tracks that remain active in the live set rather than a chronological best-of, in an interview with Side-Line.

“Vestiges” compiles known, rare and previously unreleased tracks from the project’s thirty-year catalogue, closing its twelve-track core with a previously unreleased version of “One Eyed-Man (Liber III).”

NNick Cave is bringing a piano—and an open floor for audience questions—back to North America. The Bad Seeds frontman has announced 25 dates across the U.S. and Canada for *Conversations With Nick Cave: An Evening of Talk and Music*, launching April 9 at Vancouver’s Queen Elizabeth Theatre and wrapping May 21 at New Orleans’ Saenger Theatre. The tour promises “a mixture of unvetted audience questions and intimate performances of Cave’s extensive catalog at the piano.”

The format returns to North America after its 2019 run and draws on The Red Hand Files, the correspondence project Cave started in 2018. In one early installment, a reader’s question about his breakup with PJ Harvey prompted Cave to explain how it shaped The Boatman’s Call. This October, a question about what he did on holiday led to an account of a month spent sculpting devils in clay.

Cave recalled how the original shows came together:

“Years ago, in a peculiar state of mind, I traveled across the U.S., stepped onto stages in different cities, and fielded questions from the audience. It was a strange, almost desperate idea, but those nights became deeply healing for me. I hope the audience felt the same.

Eight years have passed. The Red Hand Files have grown in reach and stature; the topics of conversation have broadened, and it feels like the right time to return to America, a different America from eight years ago, and bring the ‘Conversations…’ show back. I’ll have my piano with me, play some songs, and answer questions. What could possibly go wrong?”

The artist presale runs from Wednesday, November 11, at 10 a.m. through Thursday, November 12, at 10 p.m. General sale starts Friday, November 13, at 10 a.m., with Montréal going on sale at 11 a.m. All times are local. Register for the artist presale here.

Cave spent the summer touring the UK and Europe with the Bad Seeds behind 2024’s Wild God. At Brighton’s Preston Park, Kylie Minogue joined him for their first live rendition of “Where the Wild Roses Grow” since 2019. This month, the Bad Seeds also marked the 40th anniversary of Your Funeral… My Trial, the 1986 album that gave us “The Carny” and “Stranger Than Kindness.”

Away from the band, Cave and Bryce Dessner earned a Best Original Song Oscar nomination this year for “Train Dreams.” Cave and Warren Ellis also announced a vinyl edition of their score for The Death of Bunny Munro, the Matt Smith series adapted from Cave’s novel.

items.title: Los Angeles Post-Punk Artist Suffer Well Witnesses the Upheaval of Betrayal in “Came Around”
items.summary: You didn’t think that I’d find out, but I was in the crowd There is an awful intimacy to betrayal, particularly when the person responsible has mistaken your affection for… The post Los Angeles Post-Punk Artist Suffer Well Witnesses the Upheaval of Betrayal in
items.fullText:
You didn’t think that I’d find out,

but I was in the crowd

There is an awful intimacy to betrayal, particularly when the person responsible has mistaken your affection for an inability to see what is happening. You begin to wonder how many ordinary conversations contained a second, concealed conversation, how many reassuring gestures were merely conveniences, and whether the happiness you had begun to trust was ever shared in quite the same way. The discovery can produce an almost embarrassing clarity. Suddenly, every misplaced assurance seems to have been delivered with the confidence of someone who thought the audience had left the room.

On Came Around, Los Angeles musician and filmmaker Alex Delgado, working under the name Suffer Well, explores the uneasy interval between believing that life has finally settled into place and realizing that someone has been quietly dismantling it. Released through God Complex, the hypnotic single draws upon the romantic unease of post-punk, with Joy Division, New Order, and Interpol among Delgado’s acknowledged influences. These artists have each explored the strange compatibility of emotional distress and rhythmic discipline, finding ways to give private anxieties a physical presence.

Delgado, a singer and bassist whose creative work extends into directing and production design, oversees both the music and visual identity of Suffer Well. His multidisciplinary background suggests an interest in how a feeling can be translated into an atmosphere, a character, or a carefully arranged scene. The project occupies that fertile territory where music and cinema share an appreciation for tension, ambiguity, and the expressive possibilities of restraint.

“The song starts with finally feeling like your life is coming together, then someone comes along and upends it,’ Delgado explains.

The crowd is an inspired setting for this particular revelation. It conjures a room full of witnesses, an unsuspecting culprit, and the almost comic arrogance of somebody convinced that discretion and invisibility amount to the same thing. Delgado’s position within that gathering carries a satisfying ambiguity. He may have arrived accidentally, or perhaps suspicion had already led him there. Either possibility lends the lyrics the atmosphere of a scene from a psychological thriller, with the decisive confrontation occurring before anybody has exchanged a word.

Even the title, Came Around, accommodates several interpretations. It might describe the arrival of an unwelcome realization, the return of somebody who has caused considerable damage, or the circular movement of consequences finally catching up with their author. Each possibility carries a different emotional temperature, from resignation to vindication.

Listen to Came Around below:

For Suffer Well, these competing possibilities provide rich material. Delgado finds an uncomfortable kind of comedy in the distance between what people believe they can conceal and what others have already discovered. The song leaves us with a deliciously awkward question: once you realize that somebody has been watching, how confidently can you continue pretending there was nothing to see?

New Order have announced their first U.S. dates of 2027: a seven-show March run opening at Austin’s Moody Center and closing with two nights at the Fillmore Miami Beach. Future Islands will join the Manchester band for all three Texas dates, while Zachery Allan Starkey is billed for Austin, Fort Worth, New Orleans and Nashville. Longtime collaborator Arthur Baker will DJ both Miami Beach shows; he and New Order co-produced the band’s 1983 single “Confusion.”

The artist presale opens Tuesday, November 10, at 10 a.m. local time with the code Mojito27. General sale begins Friday, November 13, at 10 a.m. local time. Find tickets on New Order’s official tour page.

The announcement comes five days before Joy Division and New Order enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame together. The ceremony takes place Saturday, November 14, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. The Hall will honor Ian Curtis, Peter Hook, Stephen Morris, Bernard Sumner and Gillian Gilbert. After Curtis’s death in 1980, Hook, Morris and Sumner formed New Order and brought in Gilbert, carrying the urgency of Joy Division into the clubs with records like “Blue Monday.” This was their third nomination, following ballots in 2023 and 2025.

Sumner will also represent Joy Division at the ceremony. Hook, who left New Order in 2007, said in April that he planned to attend and keep his distance from his former bandmates. The day before the induction, he’ll discuss both bands at the GRAMMY Museum in Los Angeles. The recorded ceremony airs on ABC on December 8 from 8 to 11 p.m. ET/PT, then streams on Disney+ and Hulu on December 9.

New Order will play the March dates with touring musicians filling in for drummer Stephen Morris and keyboardist and guitarist Gillian Gilbert. The band said in June that the pair would step away from touring for the foreseeable future. After a September Rolling Stone interview with Morris led to reports that he was seriously ill, Gilbert clarified that he was well and that she was undergoing cancer treatment. “Thankfully, he is well. It is in fact me, who, like many other people, is living with cancer,” Gilbert wrote in a statement asking for privacy during treatment.

Before the U.S. dates, New Order will play six shows across Brazil, Chile, Argentina, Peru and Colombia, starting November 23 in São Paulo and wrapping December 9 in Bogotá. The induction follows a busy year for both catalogs. New Order remastered and expanded (The Best Of) New Order and (The Rest Of) New Order, while Joy Division’s Eternal (Live) box set collects 16 performances, including the Birmingham show where the band played “Ceremony” live for the only time. New Order made it their debut single the following year.

items.title: Aesthetische on ‘Mix The State’, Brazil’s election and the far right
items.summary: Brazilian EBM duo Aesthetische discusses the "Mix The State" EP on Alfa Matrix, Brazil's 2026 election and the rise of the far right.
items.fullText:
Brazilian EBM duo Aesthetische released “Mix The State”, a four-track EP, via Alfa Matrix on November 6, 2026. The Sao Paulo project of Fab Viscardi and Gui Pires built the digital release around its track “Break The State”, first heard on the earlier “Every Beat Matters” EP. In this interview, the duo connects the record to Brazil’s 2026 election, the country’s recent coup trial and what it calls the global rise of the far right.

Aesthetische on Brazil, democracy and the far right

SL: You’ve worked out of Sao Paulo since the Aghast View days. How much does writing a record called “Break The State” from Brazil specifically – rather than Berlin or Brussels – change what the phrase means to you?

Aesthetische: Brazil has become a Country of a large importance to the whole world given that its extension, the importance to Latam and all the natural resources and feedstocks that can be derived from the land. It is also a bio-diversity sanctuary. Obviously it would not get away without being seen as a “geopolitical force to be explored” by oligarch-ran plutocrats like the current US government, fed by the likes of terrible tech-bros and extreme right wing opportunists. Since 2018 with the rise of political movements that culminated with the ascension of Bolsonaro – a fascist at its core (and his family), the Democracy in Brazil has been at stake and if it was not for the power of the people and our institutions we would be today living in a dictatorship again. So, we (the brazilian people) at its majority Broke the State when we reelected Lula (a democratic president in 2022), resisted a coup attempt and arrested the traitors. Every single voice, every one as an individual of resistance (every beat) mattered to deviate the fate of our country to a social-political disaster. This year it happened again, the son of the traitor, a clown who worked for money to the interests of the American Government tried to get elected using his father inherited political views – and he almost did it. Fortunately the majority of the Brazilian people exploded into a democratic movement that sent millions of unlikely voters (like sick and disabled, old people and the minorities) to the voting polls and we kept the Democracy in place with a Center-Left president in place.

SL: This EP lands at the close of a bruising election year at home: a first round the right led, an October runoff that returned Lula for a fourth term, and a losing candidate who rejected the count. Did any of that bleed into the writing, or was the record finished before the campaign peaked?

Aesthetische: It was recorded before but we were aware we needed to be part of the democratic movement that took the Country by Storm, each and every individual had a very important role to move the wave towards the second round of the elections, ensuring the reelection of a democratic president.

SL: The last few years in Brazil have put the machinery of the state on full display – a former president convicted over a coup plot, courts expanding their reach, thousands of police killings, facial recognition turned on protesters. When you sing “break the state,” which state are you picturing?

Aesthetische: We are picturing the authoritarianism plutocrat right led politicians who work as new colonies to the far right power in place today in America.

SL: Some Brazilians look at that same stretch and see institutions holding the line against an attempted coup; others see a judiciary that has grown too powerful. A slogan flattens that into one raised fist. Does the nuance matter to you, or is the slogan doing a different job?

Aesthetische: Facts cannot be changed, what we do with them nevertheless, defines our future as a country and as a free and prosperous people. If you see what not holding the US president accountable for their (USA) attempted coup and the results to their country and to the geopolitical situation of the World and compare it with what Brazil did, you will get the answer I guess. You can also see what alignment to the right wing plutocrats did to Argentina. Their country is under 40% of poverty – levels never seen before, rights have been depleted from the population and the rich (even their president) getting richer by exploiting this terrible scenario.

SL: Washington weighed in this cycle – tariffs on Brazil, sanctions on judges, a US president openly backing one side. How does it feel to make anti-authority music while your country’s politics are pulled at from outside?

Aesthetische: We are trying to play our part not only as musicians but being part of a World being threatened by the rise of the Far-right.

SL: Industrial and EBM have always played with the imagery of power – uniforms, commands, martial rhythm – while claiming to oppose it. Working from a country with living memory of dictatorship, how do you stay on the right side of that line?

Aesthetische: We try to stay on the right side not letting our memories get erased (Brazil was a dictatorship before the 80s) and we had a negationist right wing fascist in power again from 2019 to 2022), defending diversity of people, of genders, of religion and raising a flag to those who are mostly in need, to those who need people to defend their rights, those that need representation because their voices are trying to be shut by selfish plutocrats who detain the economic power and are backed by a corrupt and manipulated hoard of tech bros.

The state now: apps, platforms and power

SL: For a lot of people the state they deal with daily isn’t a parliament – it’s an app, a payment rail, a face scanner, an algorithm deciding a benefit. Is that the real “alarm state” now?

Aesthetische: Yes, all of that can be used as weapons of manipulation trying to attract and mislead the masses into the fascist realm.

SL: Power has drained toward things that aren’t governments at all – platforms, payment networks, a handful of tech owners. When you aim at “the state,” are you aiming at the wrong target, or has the target simply changed shape?

Aesthetische: If you listen to our EP – “Selling Fear” – from last year – we were targeting exactly that. Fascism uses the power of the tools they have at hand to spread fear and misinformation at governmental level if that is not fought by those who know history. It is not this or that – not tech owners or the state (governments and political power) – it is exactly the alliance that can be formed by this coalition when all what matters is defending the supremacy of an economical elite – mostly driven by white male pseudo christian plutocrats. Our ep Every Beat Matters and Mix the State are a follow-up to Selling Fear.

SL: Borders, passports and deportation are hardening worldwide at the same moment capital and data cross them freely. Does the nation-state feel stronger or weaker to you than when you started making music?

Aesthetische: It is certainly different. Money and Power has always been able to get the pace of things at their favor and it has certainly contaminated the world into something we expected not to see anymore. The rise of the right, Wars taking place, coup-attempts, prejudice, white supremacism and intolerance.

A state worth defending

SL: Is there a version of “the state” you’d defend?

Aesthetische: Yes, a state that works FOR or on BEHALF of its people, its sovereignty, its culture, its social welfare, which is inclusive, free and that operates to protect our environment and to collaborate with other countries and economies on behalf of humanity. Call us utopic, but that is our vision.

SL: If a listener in Brasilia and a listener in Brussels take opposite politics from the same track, is that a failure of the song or exactly what you wanted?

Aesthetische: Well, if the listener know who we are and what we stand for it is unlikely to be on the wrong side. Political pluralism is great and wanted. What we do not tolerate is the rise of totalitarian plutocratic belic power and the oppression imposed to humanity from their representatives. Democracy should always win.

About Aesthetische

Aesthetische is a Brazilian EBM and electro-industrial duo based in Sao Paulo, formed by Fab Viscardi and Gui Pires, who had previously worked together in the Brazilian act Aghast View and in Biopsy. The duo debuted on the Belgian label Alfa Matrix in 2012 with the album “Powerswitch” and has issued a steady run of albums, EPs and singles through the label since, including “HybridCore” (2014) and “Rvprty” (2022). More recent EPs include “Boiling Over” (2023), “Confidence Is Silent” (2024), the six-track EPCD “Selling Fear” (2025) and “Every Beat Matters” (2026).

“Mix The State” extends the anti-extremism theme the duo set out on “Every Beat Matters”, reworking “Break The State” into a harsher “static noise version” and a club-focused “electric hell version” alongside the previously unreleased “Alarmstate”.

Madison, Wisconsin darkwave artist Carrellee has released a new single, “Waiting”, on November 6, 2026, with a self-directed video, ahead of a 21-date European tour opening for Dutch act Bragolin.

Carrellee wrote, performed and produced “Waiting” herself, pulling the track toward the techno and dance-pop sounds of the late 1990s and early 2000s. items.title: Anton shares video for new single ‘Serpent Des Villes’, first taste of EP ‘Tôt Ou Tard’
items.summary: Paris post-punk project Anton releases single "Serpent Des Villes" with a video, the first taste of the upcoming EP "Tôt Ou Tard" on Icy Cold Records.
items.fullText:
Paris-based post-punk project Anton has released a new single, “Serpent Des Villes”, with an accompanying video, on November 6, 2026. The track is the first single from Anton’s forthcoming EP, “Tôt Ou Tard”, on Icy Cold Records.

Anton Steinbock mixed and mastered “Serpent Des Villes” himself. Sung in French, the track pairs an organ-like synth and drum machine with wiry post-punk guitar. Its video shows Steinbock alone in a Paris park.

“Serpent Des Villes” is available now on Bandcamp and streaming platforms, including Spotify and Apple Music.

Anton’s ‘Serpent Des Villes’ follows ‘Glacier / Volcan’

Steinbock launched Anton as a solo darkwave project in Paris in 2024, releasing the debut EP “Volcan” that May. Icy Cold Records followed with “Glacier / Volcan”, covered by Side-Line in 2025, pairing that EP with new material including the track “L’Autre Destination”. Anton released the double single “Never Freed Myself” in February 2026, and “Serpent Des Villes” is the first single from the EP “Tôt Ou Tard”, also on Icy Cold Records.

About Anton

Anton is a solo darkwave project led by Paris-based musician Anton Steinbock since 2024, drawing on bands such as Joy Division and Lebanon Hanover while singing across French, German and English. The project’s debut EP, “Volcan”, arrived in May 2024, followed in March 2025 by “Glacier / Volcan” on Icy Cold Records, which combined the debut with newer material including “L’Autre Destination”. Anton played its first international shows in Italy at the end of 2025.

In February 2026, Anton released the double single “Never Freed Myself”. Side-Line covered “Glacier / Volcan” on its release. Anton’s new single, “Serpent Des Villes”, released November 6, 2026, is the first taste of the forthcoming EP “Tôt Ou Tard”, again on Icy Cold Records.

items.title: Bella Eterna releases second album ‘2Faces’, shares video for ‘When I Grow Up’
items.summary: Belgian-Spanish darkwave duo Bella Eterna releases second album "2Faces" via Mots Music, with a video for opening track "When I Grow Up".
items.fullText:
Belgian-Spanish darkwave duo Bella Eterna has released its second album, “2Faces”, via Berlin label Mots Music, alongside a video for the opening track “When I Grow Up”.

The Mots Music edition of “2Faces” lists a release date of October 30, 2026; Bella Eterna’s own Bandcamp page lists November 6, 2026. The album is out digitally and as a limited 12″ vinyl pressed in an edition of 100 black copies, with the digital edition also sold through the band’s own Bandcamp page.

“2Faces” runs nine tracks: “When I Grow Up”, “Break the Cage”, “2Faces”, “Magic Tree”, “Pink Teddy”, “Ballet For Sea Gods”, “Burn”, “When I Grow Up” (Cycle Remix by David Kano and Juanjo Reig), and “2Faces” (Parissior Remix). JG Outsider wrote, programmed and mixed the album; Gerd Van Geel wrote the lyrics and sings. It was mastered at Monoposto Mastering, with cover photography by Domingo J. Casas. The “When I Grow Up” video, set in a circus, has no credited director.

Bella Eterna pairs Van Geel, former drummer and later singer of Belgian band The Arch, with Spanish producer and DJ JG Outsider (Javier Gómez), who is based in Murcia. The project grew out of two reworkings of The Arch material: a 2020 remix of “Phantom Chase” and a 2023 revisit of “Ribdancer” for a Banshees Records tribute compilation.

Bella Eterna’s ‘2Faces’ follows 2024 debut ‘Pornographic Shadows’

Bella Eterna released its debut album, “Pornographic Shadows”, through Unknown Pleasures Records in 2024, followed by the “Fire” EP on Strict Tempo in 2025, which included an Alpha Sect remix of “Me and the Desert”. “2Faces” is the duo’s second full album and its first release through Mots Music.

About Bella Eterna

Bella Eterna was formed in Belgium by Gerd Van Geel, formerly the drummer and later lead singer of Belgian band The Arch, founded in Breendonk in 1986. Van Geel became Bella Eterna’s vocalist after producer Ludo Camberlin had band members try out The Arch’s vocal parts, and he also directed the Bella Eterna video “Mysterious Beauty”, taken from the “Fire” EP.

The project’s Spanish half, JG Outsider (Javier Gómez), is a producer and DJ born in Alicante and based in Murcia, active since 1984. He has produced for the Pink Records label since 1992, and released the 2024 track “Despierto” for Cold Transmission under the JG Outsider name.

Bella Eterna grew out of two reworkings of songs by The Arch: a 2020 remix of “Phantom Chase” and a 2023 revisit of “Ribdancer”, a track the band’s Bandcamp describes as a cult favourite in Spain, made for a Banshees Records tribute compilation. The duo released its debut album, “Pornographic Shadows”, through Unknown Pleasures Records in 2024, followed in 2025 by the “Fire” EP on Strict Tempo, which included an Alpha Sect remix of the track “Me and the Desert”.

Bella Eterna’s second album, “2Faces”, arrives via Mots Music, pairing a digital release with a limited 100-copy black vinyl edition, and is introduced by a video for its opening track, “When I Grow Up”.

items.title: Sorrow Makes a Stranger of the Self in Berlin Post-Punk Artist Rosa Damask’s Video for “Crygirl”
items.summary: I can’t understand What’s going on in my mind Sorrow can make you miss yourself. You remember how easily you once spoke to people, the plans that gave your days… The post Sorrow Makes a Stranger of the Self in Berlin Post-Punk Artist Rosa Damask’s Video for “C
items.fullText:
I can’t understand
What’s going on in my mind

Sorrow can make you miss yourself. You remember how easily you once spoke to people, the plans that gave your days direction, the feeling of being present in your own life. Losing that familiarity leaves you trying to explain a change you can barely understand, while the people who know you best seem to be speaking to someone you remember being. The distance becomes harder to bear when you start blaming yourself for it.

That estrangement runs through Crygirl, the latest single from Berlin artist Rosa Damask. Nastia Reigel, the musician behind the project, sings of a mind she struggles to understand, the effort to belong, and the sense that her old dreams have gone on without her. The refrain keeps returning to how different she feels, worrying at a realization she cannot quite account for.

The title might be an admonition muttered at her own reflection. Crygirl has the sting of a name that makes a complicated sadness sound childish, something she ought to have learned to bear more elegantly. Heard that way, it adds a second wound to the song, the shame of needing comfort when she has already begun to lose patience with herself.

Reigel’s smoky, intimate vocal carries a PJ Harvey sultriness, the words unfolding slowly over a bass line that hums and throbs. Drums land with a heavy thump, cymbals splash through the spaces around her voice, and a thick guitar riff with the romantic weight of The Cure leads into the chorus. Sighing synth pads deepen the ache, giving the refrain a weary tenderness. Her voice stays close through the swell, inviting the listener into a vulnerable moment while she is still finding the words for it.

Andrii Kaplia’s video for the song surrounds Reigel with burgundy carpets, patterned wallpaper, and gilt mirrors. In a black suit with pale ties trailing from her cuffs, Reigel crawls across the floor, folds into corners, and raises her hands beside her reflection. Her restless movements disturb the rooms’ faded formality. The mirrors keep placing another version of her in the frame, turning each private gesture into an encounter with herself.

Watch the video for Crygirl below:

Listen to Crygirl below and order the single here

Rosa Damask is the solo project of Nastia Reigel, a Berlin-based musician and producer who came up in St. Petersburg’s techno scene. She founded the queer club night Грань (Grahn’) there in 2018 and has composed music for art-house films. Rosa Damask appeared on Vatican Shadow’s Berghain Mix 09 before releasing music through his Hospital Productions label. Recordings Reigel made between 2018 and 2020 became the basis for her diary-like 2021 release on DKA, Memorials.

On Adore You, her album for Downwards Records, Reigel brought the economy of her electronic work to guitar-led post-punk. The album’s “Bored” appeared in Versace’s Fall/Winter 2025 runway show in Milan. Kaplia directed the title-track video and filmed Reigel’s live performances at Morphine Raum and Silent Space.

items.title: Belgian-Spanish Darkwave Duo Bella Eterna Let the Mask Slip on “2Faces” — Watch the Video For “When I Grow Up”
items.summary: Two faces, Heals by day, Breaks by night Morning comes, mask erased By day, the kitchen window gives you the street. Switch on the light after dark and your own… The post Belgian-Spanish Darkwave Duo Bella Eterna Let the Mask Slip on “2Faces” — Watch the Video
items.fullText:
Two faces, Heals by day, Breaks by night
Morning comes, mask erased

By day, the kitchen window gives you the street. Switch on the light after dark and your own face appears where the street was, still wearing the expression you’ve used to put other people at ease. The woman who appears in the title track of 2Faces, the second album by Belgian-Spanish darkwave duo Bella Eterna, knows that change in the light. She heals by day and breaks by night. Gerd Van Geel drops to a murmur for “By day, she paints. By night, she falls.” The smiles she paints in daylight keep her hurt out of sight. After dark, her composure gives way, and she feels the weight of what she’s spent the day covering up.

The title also refers to the two faces Domingo J. Casas photographed for the sleeve. Van Geel, the voice of Belgium’s The Arch, wrote the lyrics and sings throughout, while JG Outsider, the Spanish producer also known as Javi Golo, composed, programmed, and mixed the album. They credit 2Faces with the way each sparked new ideas in the other. For Outsider, who came up in Spanish clubs, the project was a way back to the ’80s electronics and goth that first made him want to make records. There’s more room for guitar and bass this time, and you can hear the two working as one when a bass line keeps its footing, and Van Geel lets one of his characters lose theirs.

And the night has its own myriad performances from its cast strewn across the songs of 2Faces. In one, a woman traces every step in a ballroom that’s beginning to feel like a cage. In another, a clown puts on a frightening face, yet gives himself away with the teddy bear clutched in his hand. Van Geel’s characters keep looking for a way out of the parts they’ve learned, whether that means burning the fairytale they were given or admitting what they still want. And the album’s first song asks what happens if a grown man decides he’s spent long enough acting his age.

“When I Grow Up,” the opener and lead single, begins with a bell-like figure, its rough edge hinting at guitar before reverb blurs it into something harder to name. As the drums arrive, Van Geel’s wordless cry slips into a growl, then settles into a croon with Gary Numan’s chilly poise. A rippling synth pattern keeps the song in motion while guitar notes thread through the spaces around his voice. He sings of wanting to laugh after dark and chase thunder through a world of “concrete dreams,” where there’s always a deadline pulling him back. The line “When I grow up, I want to be a child” places childhood just ahead of him, still within reach even after that choice has seemingly slipped away. The chorus rises with the abandon of someone who has already run out into the rain.

Van Geel sets the song’s video in a circus, where grown-ups make play look like work. A boy in a bowler keeps red balls aloft; a stilt walker in striped trousers looms above the troupe; a hoop spins as its performer lowers herself into a split. The clown’s painted smile remains fixed, though his eyes have already surrendered. At one point, he is rigged like a marionette, foreshadowing the dancer in the next song. In the final wide shot, he stands alone beneath the red-and-gold drapery, arms spread toward rows of empty seats.

Watch the video for “When I Grow Up” below.

The synth pads on “Break the Cage” exhale a Baroque melody, conjuring a ballroom scented with hot wax, flowers, and wine still lingering on someone’s breath. Beneath Van Geel, a supple synth bass glides as the woman in his song takes the floor, each marionette-precise step shadowed by a soul in debt. The arrangement could score the scene in Ridley Scott’s Legend where Princess Lili merges with her black gown, the rapture of the dance helping keep her ensnared. By the time Van Geel sings, “Burn the fairytale, break the cage,” the story that trapped her is the first thing she’s ready to set aflame.

On “2Faces,” a booming kick and snare dissolve into the bright sizzle of hi-hat and a scatter of handclaps. Van Geel stretches each vowel across a cool, crystalline guitar line, then sinks to a murmur as the Joker calls. A touch of Gotham enters the life of a woman who spends her days painting over cracks. Both faces wear the “Same disguise”—perhaps even the devil’s grin is just another expression she has learned to put on. When Van Geel’s voice rises again on “Lipstick, lies and gold,” you can almost see her preparing to face the room.

Low guitar tones give the synth melody in “Magic Tree” the hush and contour of a nocturne. Outsider lets the beat dissolve, then quietly restores it with a synth bass beneath Van Geel’s account of a body surrendering to the earth. First the legs go numb; soon, twigs are pushing through a human skull. Van Geel delivers the rising refrain with such composure that the bargain feels almost reasonable. The body that once could run can, at last, remain. By the time he calls himself the tree, he sounds almost at home.

In “Pink Teddy,” a clown lies beside a staged crime scene, clutching a toy bear. Outsider lends the tableau the menace of early Skinny Puppy, driven by an EBM bass sequence, low-slung synth notes, and eerie chimes. Van Geel begins submerged in reverb, then steps into the foreground with the clipped cadence of Al Jourgensen-era Ministry. The scene unfolds with the crooked logic of a Legendary Pink Dots fable—until Van Geel sings “He wanted love,” opening into a melody made for a roomful of voices. The bear remains a child’s thing in the hands of a man who has gone to considerable lengths to look frightening.

A metallic bass synth ricochets against the kickdrum on “Ballet for Sea Gods” as Van Geel sends his dancers plunging past teeth and scales. He begins with the air of someone recounting a tale handed down through generations. Then the drums crash into the refrain, and his voice gathers force until you can feel the dancers’ debt to the gods below. They dance to keep them asleep; every breath is part of the price. The tides alone bear witness.

The guitar riff on “Burn” retains its icy edge as the synths swell and the drums press in. A few notes echo Van Geel’s voice as he sings of a half-spider creature spinning a kingdom for itself in the swamp. His voice rises on “A thousand hungers burn inside,” before the chorus urges the creature to rise and fight. It already rules the mire on shattered knees—a detail that lends the command a cost. The record opened with the freedom of running out into the rain. By the end of its original tracks, simply getting to your feet in the mud demands everything you have.

After the incandescent “Burn,” David Kano and Juanjo Reig return to the album’s opening track with their “When I Grow Up” (Cycle Remix). This pared-back post-punk reprise rekindles the promise of a childhood not yet outgrown—and offers a welcome reprieve.

The final slot goes to “2Faces” (Parissior Remix), recast as ’90s-inspired electronica. The lead single and title track both return in fresh disguises, delivering one last twist on the album’s central idea: even a familiar face can still surprise.

2Faces is a perfect darkwave record, with dark synth-pop choruses that make you want to sing at full volume about the things people spend all day hiding.

The album is available digitally and on limited black vinyl through Mots Music. Listen to 2Faces below and order it here

Gerd Van Geel, also known as CUVG, started behind the drums in The Arch, the Belgian band formed in Breendonk in 1986. Producer Ludo Camberlin had the members try the vocal parts in the studio, and Van Geel wound up as the lead singer. The band’s 1990 track “Ribdancer” became a cult favorite in Spain. Van Geel also works behind the camera, directing Bella Eterna’s video for “Mysterious Beauty” from the Fire EP.

JG Outsider is Javier Gómez, the Alicante-born, Murcia-based DJ and producer also known as Javi Golo. He began DJing in 1984 and producing for Pink Records in 1992, then co-founded Essential, a label focused on vocal and progressive trance. His work as JG Outsider took him back to the EBM and industrial music that drew him in as a young DJ, territory he explored on his 2024 album Despierto for Cold Transmission.

Bella Eterna grew out of two reworkings of songs by The Arch. Outsider remixed “Phantom Chase” in 2020, then revisited “Ribdancer” for a Banshees Records tribute in 2023. The pair began writing together between Belgium and Spain, releasing their debut album Pornographic Shadows through Unknown Pleasures Records in 2024. Strictly Tempo put out Fire the following year, with Alpha Sect’s remix of “Me and the Desert”.

items.title: Richard Lloyd, Founding Member and Guitarist of Television, Passes Away at 75
items.summary: Richard Lloyd, the Television co-founder whose wiry leads made Marquee Moon a blueprint for generations of post-punk guitarists, died on Saturday, November 7, at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He… The post Richard Lloyd, Founding Member and Guitarist of T
items.fullText:
Richard Lloyd, the Television co-founder whose wiry leads made Marquee Moon a blueprint for generations of post-punk guitarists, died on Saturday, November 7, at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He was 75. His family said the cause was cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer diagnosed in March. “His loving wife Sheila and his dog Willie Mays were with him at the end,” the family said in a statement to Rolling Stone.

On “Marquee Moon,” Tom Verlaine starts with a repeating chord figure. Lloyd comes in against it, picking out two notes at a time, and Fred Smith’s bass and Billy Ficca’s drums enter in turn. Each part changes the way you hear the one before it. Lloyd takes the first solo after the second chorus, squeezes a few sharp bends into a short break, and gives the song back to the singer. Verlaine stretches out after the next chorus.

Lloyd’s ear for where a guitar should answer a singer served him well with Matthew Sweet. On Girlfriend (1991), he played the solos on “Divine Intervention” and “Evangeline.” Sweet recalled that the two took turns with the same Jazzmaster on “Evangeline,” with Sweet playing the recurring figure and Lloyd answering it before taking the solo. Lloyd returned for Altered Beast and 100% Fun. He also played on Meet John Doe, the solo debut of X’s bassist and singer.

Lloyd returned to Television for its self-titled third album in 1992 and played with the band on and off until leaving in 2007. Two years later he released The Jamie Neverts Story, an album of Hendrix covers that paid tribute to both Hendrix and Turner. He published his memoir, Everything Is Combustible, in 2017 and released The Countdown the following year.

At Baker Falls in New York City on January 23, 2026, the Richard Lloyd Group played “Alchemy” alongside Television’s “Elevation” and “Friction.” Lloyd had left the old band’s songs out of his sets for years. He spoke to Guitar World that January about what he’d set out to do with Television. “I wanted to make a dent in rock history. That was my goal, and that came true.”

Lloyd’s survivors include his wife, Sheila O’Keefe, and his son, Dylan.

items.title: Welcome to Creepsville — NYC Horror Punks The Brickbats Unearth Lost Album “Let the Goodtimes Rot”
items.summary: By the mid-’90s, goth had enjoyed about as much daylight as it could stand. Interview with the Vampire made box-office bloodsuckers of Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt in 1994, and… The post Welcome to Creepsville — NYC Horror Punks The Brickbats Unearth Lost Album “L
items.fullText:
By the mid-’90s, goth had enjoyed about as much daylight as it could stand. Interview with the Vampire made box-office bloodsuckers of Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt in 1994, and The Cure’s “Burn” opened the chart-topping soundtrack to The Crow. But by 1997, Saturday Night Live was sending up the scene with Goth Talk, a mock cable-access show that summoned the forces of darkness from the family couch.

The clubs were changing, too. At the Bank in New York, Ward 6 had already made room for industrial and EBM upstairs, with goth rock and post-punk holding down the floor below. By the end of the decade, some Los Angeles nights had pushed that crossover into techno and rave tempos. The apocalypse had acquired glowsticks and a programmable kick drum, and a whole generation of baby bats began to forget Goth’s punk roots.

But The Brickbats never forgot. The band started playing New York in 1995 with the Cramps’ rockabilly twitch, the Misfits’ gift for a gang chorus, and the Damned’s relish for a grand entrance. They brought garage-band velocity to goth nights and treated Halloween as a year-round booking, a combination that put them ahead of the early-2000s deathrock revival.  And by the time the first Drop Dead Festival came to CBGBs in 2003, singer and guitarist Corey Gorey and drummer DW Friend were on the bill with their next band, The Brides.

Gorey, Friend, and bassist Paul Morden recorded their long-lost fourth album, Let the Goodtimes Rot, with Jacques Cohen at The Space in Poughkeepsie, New York, in May and June 1999. But the record sat unfinished after the trio went on hiatus around 2000 when bassist Paul Morden headed to California to play with Gitane DeMone. Friend and Gorey salvaged the deteriorating reels and completed the songs; Gorey mixed the record, and Jeremy Hayes mastered it for its November 6, 2026 release. Twenty-seven years later, it still sounds impatient. The trio gets through thirteen songs in just over twenty-five minutes, changing pace every time you think you’ve got the measure of them.

DW Friend tumbles into the album’s title track, Let the Goodtimes Rot, with a drum fill, and Corey Gorey rakes out a jagged riff with one heel planted in old rock ’n’ roll. The refrain makes a whole-room singalong out of ejecting the guest who’s been killing the mood. Then spring-loaded guitar sets up Apt. of the Werewolf, and the bass and drums come crashing in. Gorey starts out sounding almost neighborly, then his words come quicker and give way to a howl. The rent is low enough to justify budgeting for silver ammunition. And New Yorkers have signed worse leases.

The kick drum knocks its way into Goosebumps, where a blues guitar answers Gorey’s gravelly honky-tonk drawl. The suitor offers his sweetheart a freshly extracted eyeball, then has to keep track of it when it rolls away. The guitar thickens into a steady chug and drops back into its easy swing, as if this were a perfectly ordinary second date. Friend’s next opening fill sends Too Bad Yuh Gonna Die straight into a crash of guitar, with Gorey delivering the bad news like an undertaker who’s already running behind. The refrain comes around too fast to give anyone time to argue.

On Reverb Vamplifier, the guitar tears through a surf riff, the drums keep up a merciless stomp, and the vocal melody has the lift of classic rockabilly. An icy guitar figure and a wash of keys briefly interrupt the charge, as if the secondhand amp in the song has started to act up. Its knobs are made from bones, and it houses the ghost of a roadie who died fetching Elvis a drink. The repair shop is going to have questions.

Gorey gives the King’s vowels an affectionate workout on Orange Shades, and the trio turns the bounce of “Blue Suede Shoes” into a full-tilt punk charge. The indignation over a $3.50 pair of sunglasses has the force of a man defending the deed to Graceland. More Red Wine eases into a surf saunter, with a touch of Dave Vanian’s poise circa “Eloise” in Gorey’s baritone. The song follows a woman tangoing through the small hours on Delancey Street. An altercation between her heel and a bottle of port does little to slow her down. The musicians give out first.

Friend’s opening toms summon Rock and Roll Ghost-A-Go-Go Show (Show), a Friday-night invitation to raise the dead for a three-chord set. Gorey rattles off the verses, and the chorus comes back with the weight of an Oi! gang chant. Then Theme from Frankenstein’s Hangover staggers through a bluesy surf riff like Herman Munster attempting the stairs. The beat keeps losing its footing, the guitar slides down the frets, and the monster groans as if someone has just switched on the overhead light.

The apparent hair of the dog for a monster hangover is Boozecan, where metallic percussion and clipped guitar sound like a rhythm section assembled from the empties. Gorey growls through an inventory of whiskey with a Tom Waits rasp, and the chorus takes on the swing of the Pogues as the drinkers move on to the next bar and leave the bill to management. The guitars chime over a hard, quick drumbeat on Rattle My Chains, and Gorey gives the poltergeist one of the album’s sweetest melodies. He sings the threats like a come-on. And all of a sudden, the Ouija board sounds like a singles hot line.

Creepsville takes the long way home. Gorey starts it with a gentle guitar figure that has some of the Doors’ slow, gothic sway and a curious kinship with what Interpol would play a few years later on “Leif Erikson.” The guitar syncs with Morden’s bass accentuations, leaving Gorey room to greet the town’s visitors by name and give them driving directions that end with their eyes shut. By the time the guitars bear down, the place is starting to feel like the setting of a Shangri-Las death disc or Hot Chocolate’s “Emma.” Giving the town four minutes to introduce itself lets the joke curdle into genuine unease. It’s the finest bit of pacing on the record.

We Gotta Go settles things in under a minute. A burst of Misfits-speed rockabilly finds the bartender running out of patience and daylight doing wonders for everyone’s decision-making. For a record that took twenty-seven years to get through the door, Let the Goodtimes Rot knows exactly how to make an exit.

Let the Goodtimes Rot is out now digitally and on limited-edition 12-inch vinyl. Order the album here.

The Brickbats’ original run yielded Sing You Dead, Creepy Crawly – The Unauthorized Autobiography of Undead Rock and Roll Music, and Monster Party. During the hiatus, Gorey and Friend formed The Brides with bassist Gregjaw and keyboardist Julia Ghoulia. After Morden’s death in 2006, the two returned to the stage as The Brickbats for a pair of shows in his memory in 2013, with Jason Trioxin on bass. Return of the Living Brickbats followed in 2016.

After Trioxin’s death, Gregjaw took over on bass and continued recording with the band until his death in January 2026. Gorey and Friend now work as a duo, using a rewired guitar setup to cover the low end as they write new material and prepare further catalog reissues.

items.fullText:
When synth pop embraces hell

With their song “Hell”, Never Knows Best deliv­er a dark synth pop track that clearly bears the hall­marks of dark wave and post-punk. The sound is crisp and pleas­antly bass-heavy, instantly cre­at­ing a dense atmo­sphere. I find the extremely var­ied vocals par­tic­u­larly fas­cin­at­ing; they lend the verses and the chor­us their own dis­tinct­ive, strik­ing character.

Lyrically, the song tackles themes such as self-doubt, emo­tion­al entan­gle­ments and self-imposed dark­ness, with lines like “Is this hell? We can’t find our way out / We built it ourselves” aptly reflect­ing a sense of being lost. Ultimately, this track builds on the atmo­spher­ic style that I’d already come to appre­ci­ate back in January with their release ‘Something From Nothing’, and seam­lessly main­tains that stand­ard. The res­ult is an extremely catchy synth pop track that had me hooked from the very first moment.

items.title: Red Cell – Collide And Combine
items.summary: Swedish synth pop in a nutshell: With “Collide and Combine”, Red Cell deliver a catchy, multi-layered masterpiece featuring deep baritone vocals.
items.fullText:
Analogue roots, a modern beat

Right from the very first second, Red Cell’s fant­ast­ic new song com­pletely cap­tiv­ates me. Sonically, the track reminds me fas­cin­at­ingly of greats such as Erasure and the Pet Shop Boys, though enhanced by express­ive, deep bari­tone vocals. “Collide and Combine” is extremely catchy, yet reveals a finely woven depth with every listen. Subtle effects and fresh sounds are hid­den through­out, keep­ing the track con­sist­ently engaging.

In their “The Red Cell Manifesto”, the band emphat­ic­ally stresses that they are not chas­ing any fixed style or spe­cif­ic era. Personally, how­ever, I see abso­lutely noth­ing wrong with allow­ing form­at­ive influ­ences to be so clearly felt in one’s own sound. To my ears, Red Cell simply sounds unique enough for that.

items.fullText:
Masterful reinterpretation – Thessla covers "The Things You Said"

As a loy­al Depeche Mode fan and lov­er of soph­ist­ic­ated cov­er ver­sions, I always approach rein­ter­pret­a­tions with great scep­ti­cism. Simply play­ing along isn’t enough to make an impres­sion on me.

However, this new ver­sion of this won­der­ful bal­lad from 1987 proves that there is anoth­er way. Brilliantly reima­gined, Thessla, in col­lab­or­a­tion with the sing­er MQNQ, suc­ceeds here in cre­at­ing a fas­cin­at­ing son­ic aes­thet­ic that lends synth pop an unex­pec­ted depth. The atmo­spher­ic rich­ness cap­tures the mel­an­chol­ic spir­it of the ori­gin­al and con­fid­ently brings it into the present day. On my web­site, The (Al)Most Complete Depeche Mode Covers & Tributes Archive, this suc­cess­ful track will, of course, take its right­ful place in the next update.

items.summary: Milano Flash enchants with “Bits And Pieces” through its innocent youthful charm and subtle 80s Italo-disco sounds.
items.fullText:
Electro pop with 80s charm

Right from the very first listen, Milano Flash’s ‘Bits And Pieces’ exudes a won­der­ful, inno­cent and youth­ful charm. Whilst this elec­tro-pop track from Greece may not spark a music­al revolu­tion, it pos­sesses pre­cisely the subtle qual­it­ies needed to strike a genu­ine chord. In its son­ic DNA, I’m imme­di­ately drawn in by a dis­tinct hint of 1980s Italo-disco, which lends the mel­an­chol­ic under­tone an unex­pec­tedly driv­ing, time­less lightness.

Anyone expect­ing an over­pro­duced, heavy-handed track will be sur­prised. Instead, the song car­ries an unpre­ten­tious, intim­ate aura that touches you dir­ectly and lingers in the memory.
